content.text:
Look at this project https://github.com/undrgrnd-labs/hunch take a step back and think of what we have in Maester, what our goal is and what the report provides.

How can we use this capability in Maester with the report or result we provide? How can the report be made more useful? Is there more intelligence that we can provide at run-time when the report is being genertaed? 

How can we get to the goal of Maester and produce more intelligent reporting out of the data that we have?

First assess everything and come up with a plan. Go ahead and do research. think of yourself as a very senior advanced researcher. We've got all this data we pull from a tenant. How can we improve the report. Can we ask a person what they are looking for and fine tune the report?

The goal is to make Maester and the report very invaluable, provide insights that are not already there.

items.content: Review Maester's goal, data and current report

Maester 3.0 (RFC maester365/maester discussion 2050) design was drafted on 2026-10-02 in worktree `.claude/worktrees/maester-3-planning-6643a9` (branch `claude/maester-3-planning-6643a9`), as untracked files: `docs/proposals/maester-3.0-design.md` plus `docs/proposals/maester-3.0-evidence/` (idmap.csv, authorship-seed.csv, Windows PowerShell 5.1 probe script). Nothing is implemented or committed yet.

Core shape: `Test.<ID>.ps1` + `.md`; `[MtTest]` PowerShell-class attribute with 16 properties read from the AST; engine-owned service/licence gates; run config = superset of `maester-config.json` passed by discovery or `-Config`; Pester kept as a compatibility provider; result JSON stays 2.x-shaped with additive fields; single-threaded with parallel-readiness rules.

**Why:** Merill asked for the design first, implementation after his rulings. The design went through a three-proposal panel and a 61-finding red-team pass.

Rulings Merill gave on 2026-10-03: remove the Pester dependency in 3.0 (maester-action installs Pester as an explicit step); accepted risk stays cloud-only; land on `main`; strip the boilerplate try/catch and connection/licence guards from tests (engine handles them); tests expose parameters with a UI "kind" (`[MtParameter(Kind)]`, plugin registry); add a `Platform` attribute; design must leave room for container fan-out; he wants the engine choice made on stability for parallel runs, not on the RFC. Design now recommends a small C# scheduling core (`Maester.Engine.dll`) inside the module, single-threaded by default in 3.0.

Further rulings (same day): PowerShell 7 only (manifest 7.4/Core, 5.1 CI leg removed); attribute is `[MaesterTest]` / `[MaesterParameter]` (commands keep the `Mt` prefix); the four author corrections are accepted; `Convert-MtTest` custom-test converter ships in 3.0; built-ins always run with `-SkipBuiltIn` for custom-only.

Merill approved the C# scheduling core (`Maester.Engine.dll` inside the module, single-threaded by default in 3.0).

**Implementation status (2026-10-06):** M0, M1 and M2 are committed and pushed to draft PR maester365/maester#2334 (branch `claude/maester-3-planning-6643a9`). Merill ruled: no 2.x release; keep pushing to the draft PR; maester-action changes stay out of this repo. Engine source `src/Maester.Engine` (net8.0, committed DLL verified byte-for-byte by CI; source revision is excluded from the version so builds are reproducible). Built-ins ship in `builtin-pester/`; module version is 3.0.0. Still open with Merill: how Pester `Inconclusive` maps; `exit`/`break` in a native test proposed as Error/TestError. Next step is M3 (native tests end to end).

**Status update (2026-10-06, later):** M3–M9 are all done and pushed to PR 2334, including code and security reviews (all findings fixed). Every built-in check (746) is native; Pester is optional; 67 exported commands; docs, report app and test-docs generator updated. Pending owner sign-off: the list of design changes given to Merill (unexported check functions, Medium default severity for 59 checks, -Tag All semantics, catch-all removal turning skips into TestError, MT1060→MT.1060, Pester Inconclusive left as in 2.x, making `verify-dll` a required branch check). Open follow-up: about 60 checks still have inline licence guards that should become CompatibleLicense (a task chip was offered).

**How to apply:** Before more work, check what Merill ruled on that list; then pushing to PR 2334; sync with `main` through the app before pushing when the PR conflicts. Research reports with maester-cloud internals were deliberately NOT copied into the public repo — see [[contributors-attribution-system]] for the attribution system the authorship seed replaces.

**Layout ruling (2026-10-09):** Merill approved the full repo re-layout on PR 2334 (commits 26b52d3e renames, 2accf394 fixes): lowercase kebab-case folders, XSPM nested at tests/maester/xspm, public/{run,connect,report,app,services/<service>}, internal/{engine,session,connect,report,app,services/<service>,checks/<suite>/<service>,generated/{eidsca,orca},utility}, user folder `custom/` (old `Custom/` still accepted). Rules live in website/docs/contributing.md#repository-layout and AGENTS.md; enforced by powershell/tests/general/RepositoryLayout.Tests.ps1 (including dangling-path check). New services must be added to the guide, AGENTS.md and that test. Ruling (same day): folders name products, cross-cutting themes are tags; ai-agent became copilot-studio (commit e83ee3aa), AI tag added to MT.1113-1122 and MT.1223, copilot and foundry reserved. Helpers become available to custom tests only by moving to public/services/<service>/ and exporting (procedure in the contributing guide).

**Attribute rename (2026-10-09):** Merill renamed `[MaesterTest(CompatibleLicense = ...)]` to `License` before release (commit d59e5959 on PR 2334, DLL rebuilt; no alias). This overrides the earlier design-doc ruling to keep the ZTA name. PR 2334 was marked ready for review the same day.

**Engine review (2026-10-10/11):** a subagent reviewed src/Maester.Engine and powershell/internal/engine at 48c28c8c; all seven findings are fixed on PR 2334 (c5f3976e, 584c11d2) with regression tests. The console renderer/dashboard was written afterwards and has not been code-reviewed. `Product` on [MaesterTest] is a single string; built-ins must use a name from Products in MaesterTestSchema.psd1 (NativeTestLint.Tests.ps1 enforces list membership, exact case, and folder-to-product mapping). Merill asked whether Product is an array; it is not, and he has not asked to change it. Other sessions (console/perf, runspace investigation) push to the same PR branch: fetch and fast-forward before every edit, and message them after pushing.

**Maintainer review (2026-10-11):** SamErde reviewed PR 2334 at 22ceb197 (AI-assisted) and found four issues, all fixed in a3ed24bd6 with tests: the tenant config file is resolved in the single config pass at the start of Invoke-Maester (Get-MtConfigTenantId, mockable in tests); instance rows set Parameters/TimeoutSeconds per instance, merged over the family row; a family's instance source runs as an engine item under the family's timeout; single-file -Path reads the sibling suite.json. Review threads are answered with a one-line reply and resolved.

**Design doc synced 2026-10-14** (PR 2334 merged to main 2026-10-14; the sync commit b34ea4ef2 landed after, so it is on PR maester365/maester#2386 from branch `claude/maester-3-design-sync`): status = implemented (M0–M9 minus soak/release); -Tag All/Full removed (error); Pester Inconclusive→Skipped; report keeps 2.x layout + dry-run notice + typed attributes; suite.json `NoResultReason`; maester-action opt-in `maester_major_version: "3"`; §12.2 now points to the Maester Packs design (PR 2358); section 16 has a "Ruled during implementation" list. **`MP.` is now a reserved test ID prefix in 3.0** (schema, New-/Convert-MtTest, Invoke-Maester warnings, website test builder, writing-tests docs) — see [[maester-marketplace-design]].

Redesign of how Maester tests are grouped and mapped to MITRE ATT&CK and frameworks. Started as research on 2026-10-11; the same day Merill told me to implement it.

**Research (private):** maester-cloud branch `claude/test-taxonomy-research` (commit 348d21c6, local only, not pushed), worktree `/Users/merill/github/maester-cloud/.claude/worktrees/test-taxonomy-research`, folder `docs/test-taxonomy-research/` (`clean-slate-attribute-design.html` is the design review; vendor survey; `notes/`). **Implementation (Maester):** branch `claude/maester-3-test-attributes`, stacked on the 3.0 branch (`claude/maester-3-planning-6643a9`, PR 2334), worktree `/Users/merill/github/maester/.claude/worktrees/maester-3-test-attributes`. Local commits only; not pushed, no PR. Contract files: `docs/proposals/maester-3.0-test-attributes.md` (design), `website/docs/writing-tests/attribute-rubric.md` (rubric), `powershell/assets/MaesterTaxonomy.psd1` (products/features/areas/resource types), `powershell/assets/MaesterAttackTechniques.json` (ATT&CK 19.2 trimmed).

**Owner rulings (2026-10-11):**
- OK to change the existing `Category` and `Tag`.
- Research must NOT go into the Maester repo; maester-cloud is fine. Only the final redesign goes into Maester.
- A test can span products (e.g. Entra ID and Intune): handled with single `Product` + optional `RelatedProduct` list.
- Fill in values for all tests; define a rubric per attribute; add unit tests that fail when a test does not meet the rubric.
- Add a review step where an AI reviewer checks new or changed test attributes against the rubric and fails otherwise; he will supply an API key (I defaulted to the Claude API, secret `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, model `claude-opus-5-5`; the repo's only earlier AI script used Gemini as a one-off).
- Maester Cloud (closed source, `jozrahq/maester-cloud`) is his hosted product, positioned against Tenable/Wiz; keep it out of public Maester docs.

**Design as implemented in the spec:** remove `Category` (result `Block` derived from Product) and `Preview` (→ `Lifecycle`); `Tag` = owner's free labels, built-ins carry none; 2.x tags keep selecting through `Maester.LegacyTags.json`; `Product` is a registry key; new `RelatedProduct`, `Feature`, `Area`, `ResourceType`, `UserImpact`, `ImplementationCost`, `Mitre`, `Control`, `Permission`, `Lifecycle`, `ReplacedBy`; typed selectors `-Product/-Feature/-Area/-Severity/-Suite`; `suite.json` `Frameworks` + framework files for CIS/CISA.

**Things I learned that are easy to lose:**
- The Zero Trust Assessment public repo has no written rubric (only ValidateSet values); I calibrated on its 336 tests (risk High 60/Med 35/Low 6; user impact Low 66/Med 27/High 7; cost Low 54/Med 37/High 9). Merill believes a ZTA rubric exists; ask him for it if alignment matters.
- 27 of the 31 CISA `MS.EXO.*` policies missing from ScubaGear were moved to `MS.SECURITYSUITE.*` (4 removed, 4 not found); ScubaGear's migrations CSV has the map.
- Every Maester severity is Maester's own (2.x `tests/maester-config.json` rows, carried unchanged into the `Severity` attribute). Upstream ratings exist but are overridden: EIDSCA `Severity` (26 of 44 differ) and ORCA's check weight `ChiValue` (only 15 of 54 agree). CISA has SHALL/SHOULD only; CIS has Level/profile only. Summary for the EIDSCA team (Merill to share upstream, not posted by me): https://claude.ai/artifact/4wBJt6jQLEZhfR2Pafd8xZ and `eidsca-severity/` in the research folder (commit a6efdb43); upstream repo `Cloud-Architekt/AzureAD-Attack-Defense`, branch `AADSCAv4`.
- Severity lesson (Merill, 2026-10-11): he reads the rubric's High as covering a missing control that protects users from phishing-type attacks, and pushed back when I recommended Medium for EIDSCA Highs. My reading after re-evaluating: a phished/sprayed password is NOT "another weakness first"; the main control against such an attack is High (number matching), second layers stay Medium. Use ZTA `RiskLevel` (clone of `microsoft/zerotrustassessment`) as a per-test reference when rating Entra checks: Maester's EIDSCA values match ZTA on 18 of 24 shared settings. Details and changed proposals: `eidsca-severity/re-evaluation.md` in the research folder. Rubric wording for this is proposed, not applied.
- The 3.0 branch is being pushed to by other sessions; base new work on `origin/claude/maester-3-planning-6643a9`, not the old local worktree.

**State (2026-10-12):** PR maester365/maester#2362 (branch `claude/maester-3-test-attributes`) was MERGED into the 3.0 branch (PR 2334) on 2026-10-12 with a merge commit (`4fa510d45`), at Merill's request. It carried: typed attributes + rubric + AI review step; 135 severity changes; framework mapping through `Control` only (framework files are catalogues, no `Tests`/`IdPrefix`); 309 NIST SP 800-53 mappings (Sonnet agents, 66 low-confidence ones left out, none human-reviewed) with pinned `MaesterNistControls.json`; website test builder at `/test-builder` (Radix/cmdk shadcn-style controls, licence explorer, daily licence-plan workflow); beginner doc `first-custom-test.md`; preview versions numbered `3.0.0-previewN` then `3.0.0`. Still open: 8 held severity proposals; 66 low-confidence NIST mappings; `Permission` values; `website/docs/tests/` regeneration; live run of the review script (needs `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` secret + `attribute-review-override` label); first preview publish should produce `3.0.0-preview1` (unverified); suite tags are no longer in a result's `Tag` (I changed a 3.0-branch test for this; Merill has not ruled). Preview: `.claude/launch.json` in the main checkout has `website-test-builder` (port 3111). The EIDSCA summary artifact is shared by link: ask before republishing. maester-cloud research branch is local only (`93c64e24`).

**How to apply:** check `git -C <worktree> log` for how far the implementation got before continuing. Don't push or open a PR unless asked. Further research goes to the maester-cloud folder. See [[maester-3-design]], [[maester-marketplace-design]].

Drafted 2026-10-07 in worktree `.claude/worktrees/maester-3-planning-6643a9`: `docs/proposals/maester-packs-design.md`, on branch `claude/maester-packs-design`, draft PR maester365/maester#2358 stacked on the 3.0 branch (#2334); retarget to main after 3.0 merges. Site mockup canvas: https://claude.ai/artifact/9frFAaGEGJgDRXvyst8Ht1 (private).

Owner rulings (2026-10-07): names **pack** / **Maester Packs**; domain **packs.maester.dev** (maester.dev DNS is on Cloudflare); site + small Worker API (+ D1) on Cloudflare, indexing/scanning in GitHub Actions on a public repo (free minutes), keep costs ~$0–5/month; **binaries allowed** but flagged High risk (risk levels Low/Medium/High/Blocked, like skills.sh audits); **v1 runs packs in-process** (isolation via containers later; keep the hosted-service angle generic in public docs); **no verification programme in v1** — badges instead: Official, Microsoft MVP (from the MVP directory API the `merill/newsletter` repo syncs, `app/src/lib/server/authors/mvp-api.ts`), GitHub-verified org. Publisher-side scanners (Codacy/CodeRabbit) shown only as "repository signals".

Design review of 2026-10-07 fully folded in (fork-commit reachability, single loader gate, packs can't pose as built-ins, namespaced connector services `<CODE>.<Platform>`, -IncludePackScopes/MissingScope, phase-1 blocklist with serial/expiry/offline root key, split scan/publish indexer, **no archive mirror (Merill ruled: never cache repos in Cloudflare; a pack gone from GitHub is skipped — NotRun `PackUnavailable` + report warning)**, lifecycle states, numeric IDs, ID ledger, pack API contract, AllSigned/WDAC, terms/takedowns, /p/ routes, maester365 code `MAES`).

**Why:** Merill wants to review the full design before implementation.

Pack test IDs are `MP.<code>.<number>` (e.g. MP.CNT.0001): `MP.` reserved prefix, 2–5 char code (letters/digits, starts with a letter) held by the **publisher (GitHub user/org, numeric owner ID)**, claimed at the first index of any of its repos, first come first served — no PR; one code per owner, permanent, shared by all its packs (index keeps IDs unique across them); every not-listed version gets an indexing status with reason + fix (doc 7.7, packs.maester.dev/status/{owner}/{repo}, Test-MtPack -Remote); `Find-MtPack -Code` / packs.maester.dev/codes/<CODE> lookup; anti-squat: account >30 days, one claim/day, unlisted claims lapse after 90 days. Also ruled: list on first passing install (owner account >30 days), **one new pack per owner per day**, Astro, High-risk packs shown by default, MVP API best-effort, first official pack Google Workspace.

**Under discussion (2026-10-08, community feedback from TestimoX and LeastPrivilegedMSGraph; NOT yet in the design doc — Merill wants the doc updated only after the Discord discussion ends):** outside tools run as their own step and the pack's connector only reads the output file (no signing; schema-version + max-age checks); **hybrid module-backed packs** (code in the publisher's PowerShell module, pack = manifest + build-generated static catalog + docs, `RequiresModules` + `Provider {Module, ApiVersion}`; chosen over Gallery-hosted packs so GitHub/MVP badges still validate); Maester never installs modules (generated `Install-Module` command; missing → tests skipped); publisher Setup tab; rule catalogs; coverage as own result (`NotCollected`, opt-in CI); own auth libs wrapped as connectors + run-scoped cache; permissions beyond Graph (Entra/Azure RBAC/Exchange roles, `MissingPermission`); connection targets via `Connections.<Service>`/parameter kinds/families. Mode names proposed: code = **Script pack** / **Module pack**; data = **Live** / **Import** / **Collect** (optional Collect hook once per run + Release hook, off by default). Summarised (with two SVG diagrams) in the overview HTML's "Under discussion" section.

**How to apply:** Only owner-side setup is still open (GitHub App, signing key, Cloudflare). Never raise or record the existing `InvokeMaester` PostHog run telemetry in the Packs design — Merill ruled it out of scope (opt-out is already documented). Don't implement until he rules. Keep maester-cloud internals out of public docs, as with [[maester-3-design]].

If you're curious, `noul` is Jev's name for a yes/no question (from Ber`noul`li distribution), meaning "probability of yes". - **Teacher:** the model you would otherwise call for every question, such as a decision model (Clef, Jev, etc) or an LLM-as-judge (frontier model or otherwise). - **Student:** hunch's small classifier for one question, which reads an embedding of the state from EmbeddingGemma 2. - **State:** what you're asking the question about. - **Graduation:** where hunch starts answering on its own (cross-validation on the teacher's answers shows it agrees with the teacher often enough) - **Audit:** after graduation, some of the student's answers also go to the teacher to check up. hunch trains the student on the teacher's judgements and then takes over once it is confident enough. ## Why (... and why we built it!) You keep your judge in the loop, but you call it less! - **Cheaper and faster.** hunch can take a lot of the load off the more expensive judge. See [hunch/README.md](hunch/README.md#performance). - **eg2cpu:** encoding a 32-token text to layer 8 (an optimized path hunch often takes), takes about 0.6 ms per text in batches on a 24-core Sapphire Rapids server with AMX. result.output:
# hunch

hunch is a proxy: it sits in front of a /v1/systemone model you might already be using to answer questions about textual data (like
"did this tool call fail in this agent trace?", "is this log entry from a hacker?"). It learns to answer the easy questions itself, but way faster,
making your whole system more responsive (and sometimes smarter too!).

- **The teacher** either an LLM judge or a dedicated decision model. This is what hunch learns from.
- **The student** is hunch's own classifier model, one per question: Once cross-validation on the teacher's answers
  shows the student agrees with the teacher often enough, the question *graduates* and the student answers it.
- **A state** what we ask questions about: e.g. a tool call and its output, a message (or really any JSON).

A question has a type:
- `noul`: yes or no (the question protocol's name for it), answered as P(yes);
- `choice`: one of named options, given as `criteria` (option name -> description);
- `score`: one of ordered levels, given as `criteria` (a list, lowest first).

## Quick start

```bash
python -m hunch serve --db proxy.db --backend http://teacher.example/v1/answer   # listens on 127.0.0.1:8765
```

```bash
curl -s localhost:8765/v1/answer -d '{"state": {"call": "bash: ls config/", "output": "ls: config/: No such file or directory"},
  "questions": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the tool call fail?"}}}'
```

```json
{"answers": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.97, "answered_by": "backend"}}, "answered_by": "backend", "model": "teacher"}
```

`answered_by` lets you know who got it: `backend` (the teacher), `proxy` (the student) or `cache` (previously answered, reused).

A question with options looks like this:

```json
{"type": "choice", "instructions": "What kind of output is this?",
 "criteria": {"test_run": "Output of running tests", "build": "Output of a build or compile", "other": "Anything else"}}
```

## The teacher

hunch sends a `POST` request to the teacher, `{"state": ..., "questions": {id: question}}`, and expects
`{"answers": {id: answer}}` back, with an answer for every question:
- `noul`: `{"type": "noul", "noul": 0.97}`, P(yes);
- `choice`: `{"type": "choice", "probabilities": {"test_run": 0.9, "build": 0.05, "other": 0.05}}`;
- `score`: `{"type": "score", "probabilities": {"0": 0.1, "1": 0.7, "2": 0.2}}`, by level index.

hunch's returns the same response, plus `choice` or `score` and `confidence` fields.

 - `--backend`: is the teacher's URL. 
 - `--backend-header 'Authorization: Bearer …'`: adds headers to the teacher's requests, and
 - `--backend-timeout` (default 30 s) sets a timout.

Teacher problems turn into a 502 for the caller: an error, a timeout, a missing question or an answer hunch can't
parse.

## How it decides

For each request, in order:
1. **The store.** If the store already holds an answer for this exact state and every question, hunch returns it. The
   answer is a label or the teacher's last answer.
2. **The students.** The students answer if all of these are true: every question has graduated, its student is
   confident, and the state is not novel. A novel state is unlike the examples the student learned from.
3. **The teacher.** Otherwise the whole request goes to the teacher. The teacher reads the state once for all
   questions. Every answer becomes a training example.

The store is read by the hash of the state's text, so a stored answer needs no encoding. And when a question in the
request hasn't graduated, or is demoted, the request is bound for the teacher whatever its features say: hunch asks
the teacher at once and encodes the state at the same time, for learning and audits. Until a question graduates, a
request then takes as long as the slower of the two, not both one after the other.

**Graduation.** A refit retrains a question's student and cross-validates it on its examples. The question
graduates in one of two modes:
- **symmetric:** on the states it is confident enough to answer, the student agrees with the teacher at least 90% of
  the time, and on at least 80% of the answers other than the most common one (both the 95% lower bound);
- **one-sided** (`noul` only): the student answers only when it is confident the answer is "no", and passes every
  likely "yes" to the teacher. This needs at most 2% of its "no" answers to be wrong, and at least 85% of the teacher's
  "yes" answers to be passed on. It suits rare, important answers, such as "is this an injection?".

A question refits on a worker thread once it has 100 new examples (`--refit-every`). The system checks the count each
time it records the answers of the teacher. Requests keep the previous fit until the new fit is swapped in. `train`
with `"refit": true` (the default) refits before it responds. With `"refit": false`, its examples count toward the
next check. The refit then waits for the next answer from the teacher. The refits of one question run one at a time.
The fit in use is therefore always from the newest examples. Fits are kept in the store, so a restarted proxy answers
at once.

**Audits.** Graduated questions keep being checked against the teacher:
- 10% of the students' answers (`--audit`) are also sent to the teacher, in the background: the client gets the
  student's answer without waiting. If the teacher is down, the audit fails, not the request.
- Every request that goes to the teacher anyway also checks each student that would have answered it.

A question is demoted while its last 100 audits are significantly below its bar. The bar is: agreement below 90%
(symmetric), or more than 2% of "no" answers wrong (one-sided). While a question is demoted, its requests go to the
teacher. The question answers again when its audits recover. The store keeps the audits, so a demoted question stays
demoted after a restart. A refit that changes its mode starts a new window, because the old audits measured the other
mode. The thresholds and their statistics are in [../docs/glossary.md](../docs/glossary.md#the-proxy-hunch).

Which questions can graduate at all is the subject of [../docs/question-design.md](../docs/question-design.md).

## Training: `POST /v1/train`

You can also give hunch answers directly:

```json
{"question": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the tool call fail?"},
 "cases": [
   {"state": {"call": "bash: ls config/", "output": "ls: config/: No such file or directory"}, "answer": true, "kind": "labelled"},
   {"state": "added 214 packages in 6s", "answer": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.04}, "kind": "sampled"}],
 "refit": true}
```

- **`sampled`** answers are treated as the teacher's, for example answers collected from its logs. hunch keeps the
  newest 2,000 per question (`--sampled-cap`), together with the answers it forwards, and weights each by its
  confidence.
- **`labelled`** answers are ground truth: benchmark labels, harness flags, human review. hunch keeps the newest
  5,000 of each class per family (`--labelled-cap`); they weigh twice as much as a sampled answer, and win over a
  sampled answer for the same state. They are how a student learns
  past a teacher's blind spot (`../examples/injection_teacher/`).
- **`answer`** can be a label (`true`/`"yes"`/`1` for `noul`, an option name for `choice`, a level index or legend
  entry for `score`), P(yes) as a bare number for `noul` (`0.04`), a list of probabilities in option order
  (`[p_yes]` for `noul`), or an answer object. Probabilities must be in [0, 1]; a request with any invalid answer
  gets 400, and none of its cases are kept.

Each state counts once per question. A new answer for a state replaces the old answer. The response is the status of
the question after the refit.

For each labelled state, hunch also keeps the teacher's answer. This lets hunch measure the teacher against ground
truth. If the teacher has already answered the state, hunch keeps that answer. If not, hunch asks the teacher in the
background. It makes one call per state, which covers every version of the question it knows. `--no-ask-for-labels`
turns those calls off. Answers that arrive later through traffic are still kept. The question's status reports how
many labels have a teacher answer (`labels_with_teacher`).

### Teacher tuning

Those pairs let hunch tune the teacher. An LLM judge often ranks well but puts its cut points in the wrong place. In
the examples, a judge that separated prompt injections with AUC 0.96 scored 0.62 accuracy at its default 0.5. At each
refit, a question version with at least 50 labels that have a teacher answer fits a recalibration of the teacher. The
recalibration is a logistic regression on the log-probabilities of the teacher, with each class weighted equally.
5-fold cross-validation then compares it with the raw teacher, answer by answer. Tuning switches on only if it
significantly improves balanced accuracy, which counts each class equally. It must also not significantly lower plain
accuracy. The balanced test stops the tuning from winning by never predicting a rare class. The plain test stops a
class seen only a few times from carrying the tuning.

When tuning is on, every answer from the teacher is recalibrated. This includes an answer that was just forwarded and
an answer replayed from the store. The original answer of the teacher stays under `untuned`. To see whether tuning is
on, and why, read the status of the question under `report.tuning`.

Students then aim at the tuned answers, in two tiers. At each refit, hunch fits two students:
- **Full:** Learns the answers of the tuned teacher. Once it graduates, it answers.
- **Partial:** Learns the own answers of the teacher, but is graded against the tuned answers. It answers only until
  the full student graduates.

Grading the partial student against tuned answers keeps it to the states where tuning didn't change the answer.
Those are usually most of them: clear successes and clear failures, far from either cut point. States near the
moved cut point go to the teacher.

Audits compare against the tuned answer. Every local answer says which tier answered (`tier`). The question's status
does the same.

Tuning only moves the cut points. It does not make the teacher see things it misses. A student trained on labels with
the features of EG2 can learn past a blind spot. A recalibrated teacher cannot.

### Blind spots

`GET /v1/questions/{key}/blind_spots` (or `proxy.blind_spots(question)`) shows where the teacher disagrees with your
labels. It uses the tuned teacher when tuning is on. It reads only what the store already has, so it makes no teacher
calls:
- **Summary:** the accuracy of the teacher on the labels, raw and as served, a confusion matrix of label against the
  answer of the teacher, and recall for each label. A label that the teacher never predicts shows up here.
- **Spots:** the disagreements, grouped by (label, answer of the teacher) and clustered by EG2 features. The largest
  and most confidently wrong are first. Each spot gives its size, the probability of the teacher for the label, and
  the share where an out-of-fold student agrees with the label. A high share suggests a real blind spot. A low share
  suggests label noise, or a question that the labels and the teacher read differently.
- **What to label next:** for each spot, the number of unlabelled states from traffic that the teacher answered the
  same way within the radius of the spot, and the nearest few. They show whether a spot is a handful of cases or a
  large part of your traffic.

States come with their text when hunch keeps texts (`--store-text`). Otherwise, they come as hashes. The endpoint can
return stored texts. So it needs the training token when a token is set.

On the pi stream, the largest spot is searches that find nothing. The stream uses Clef's severity answers, 400 of our
labels, and the other 1,600 results as traffic. The rubric calls these searches minor. Clef calls them none. Several
hundred traffic results look alike. That is a wording problem, not a model problem. The clearest true blind spot is
GitHub issue text that describes errors. Clef reads it as a failure. The student backs the labels that say it is not
a failure.

## Rewording questions: versions and families

A question's *version* is its type, instructions and criteria, so a reworded question is a new version: it starts with
no sampled answers and no graduation, because the teacher's answers to one wording aren't answers to another. To keep
ground truth across rewordings, name the question's family:

```json
{"type": "noul", "family": "injection", "instructions": "…reworded…"}
```

- Every version in a family uses the labelled examples of the family. A new wording can therefore graduate before it
  has seen a single teacher answer.
- A version trained without a family joins one, with its labels, the first time a question names it.
- Versions in a family must have the same type and options. Otherwise their labels mean different things.
- A request may leave the family out once a version is known.

## Running it

| endpoint | |
|---|---|
| `POST /v1/answer` | a request (above) |
| `POST /v1/train` | training cases (above) |
| `GET /v1/questions` | `{"ready", "stats", "latency", "layer", "encoder", "states", "questions": [...]}`: request counts, latency by who answered, and each question's examples, graduation, cross-validation report and audits |
| `GET /healthz` | 200 while the process is up |
| `GET /readyz` | 200 once every question restored from the store has a fit, else 503 |

- **Access:** `--token` (or `$HUNCH_TOKEN`) makes every endpoint but `/healthz` and `/readyz` require
  `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `--train-token` (or `$HUNCH_TRAIN_TOKEN`) gives `/v1/train` its own token, since
  training writes ground truth. Without a token the server is open, so keep it on `127.0.0.1` (the default `--host`).
- **Limits:** request bodies over `--max-body` (1 MiB) get 413, and a POST without a valid `Content-Length` gets 411
  or 400; the token is checked before the body is read. A client that sends nothing for `--client-timeout` seconds
  (30), idle or mid-request, is disconnected. At most `--max-connections` (64) connections are served at once, each
  on its own thread; one more gets 503.
- **Errors:** an unexpected failure gets 500 with only an `error_id`; the detail is logged to stderr under that id.
- **CPU:** `--threads` caps the threads the encoder uses (the default is every core).
- **Logs:** `--access-log` writes one line per request to stderr: method, path, status, milliseconds, who answered.

**Storage.** `--db` takes a SQLite path, or a Redis URL (`redis://host:port/db?prefix=name`, with
`pip install hunch[redis]`). The store holds:
- each state once, by the hash of its text: its layer-8 features (2 KB) and, with `--store-text`, the text;
- each question's examples (one per state), its latest fit and its last 100 audits;
- the encoder fingerprint: the checkpoint revision, layer, matmul precision and clipping that computed the features.
  A proxy with a different encoder refuses the store; with `--store-text`, `--rebuild` re-encodes the stored states
  and refits every question on the new features.

Several processes can share a Redis store, but each keeps its own students and refit counters. They share examples,
fits and the audits they record. Each process reads the audits only when it starts, so their demotions can differ.

**State text.** The encoder and the teacher read a state as its text: a tool call and its output as `call\noutput`,
followed by any other fields as `name: value` lines, and any other JSON as sorted JSON. The encoder reads at most 1,024
tokens, so a state over 3,000 characters is clipped to its head and tail, keeping the end of a long output, where an
error usually is.

## Performance

Measured on an Apple M5 Pro with the real encoder, on real tool results of about 190 tokens (one question per
request, the teacher replayed with a 500 ms delay):

| | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|
| answered by the student, one request at a time | 22 ms | 51 ms | 76 ms |
| answered by the teacher | 531 ms | 579 ms | 583 ms |

Audited answers return as fast as other student answers. The audit happens afterwards.

Concurrent requests share the encoder: one thread encodes whatever is waiting as one batch. Throughput rises with load,
and latency under load is mostly the wait for the current batch:

| concurrent callers | requests/s | p50 | p95 | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 41 | 21 ms | 47 ms | 71 ms |
| 4 | 51 | 83 ms | 122 ms | 137 ms |
| 16 | 73 | 226 ms | 294 ms | 301 ms |
| 32 | 86 | 382 ms | 451 ms | 466 ms |

- **CPU and memory:** a single caller keeps about 7 cores busy while a request is encoded. `--threads` caps that. The
  process holds about 1.5 GB, the model included.
- **Restart:** a restarted proxy is ready at once. It answers from the kept fits.
- **Cost per request** is mostly the encoder pass to layer 8. It grows with the length of the state, up to the
  1,024-token limit. The encoder's own numbers, batched and per hardware, are in
  [../docs/performance.md](../docs/performance.md).

## From Python

```python
from hunch import HTTPBackend, Proxy

proxy = Proxy(backend=HTTPBackend("http://teacher.example/v1/answer"), db="proxy.db")
proxy.answer({"state": {"call": "...", "output": "..."}, "questions": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "..."}}})
proxy.train(question, cases)       # as POST /v1/train
proxy.predict(question, states)    # the student's answers for many states, without routing or learning
proxy.wait()                       # until pending refits and background audits are done
```

Custom stores implement `hunch.Store`.

## Live images: `hunch.live`

The proxy answers questions about text states behind a teacher. `hunch.live` answers questions about a stream, from
one EG2 embedding per item. It learns from the items that a person or a teacher labels as it runs. An item is an
image or a text. An image is, for example, a webcam frame (about 110 ms on an Apple M5 Pro's CPU at 70 soft tokens).
A text takes about 12 ms for a short tool result, by the full pass, so it shares the space of the prompts.

```python
from hunch.live import Choice, Detector, Eyes, Watcher

eyes = Eyes(tokens=70)
seen = Choice(eyes, {"nothing": ["a person with empty hands"], "mug": ["a person holding up a mug"]},
              quiet={"nothing"}, empty="nothing", new=lambda name: [f"a person holding up a {name}"])
fire = Detector(eyes, yes=["a photo of fire"], no=["a normal indoor photo"], threshold=-0.04)

x, ms = eyes.see(jpeg)            # or eyes.see("bash('npm test') -> 'Error: Timeout of 2000ms exceeded'")
seen.ask(x)                     # {"name", "p", "state": quiet | sure | unsure, "probs", "zero", ...}
seen.teach(x, "seashell")       # a new answer, with new("seashell")'s prompts; the student refits in the background
seen.forget()                   # back to the answers it started with
watcher = Watcher(seen, teacher)  # teacher(jpeg, names) -> {name or hunch.live.ELSE: probability}
watcher.look(jpeg, x, seen.ask(x))
```

- Every answer starts out zero-shot, from its text prompts. When you label frames, a logistic regression learns from
  them. The trust in it depends on how much a new frame looks like the frames it learned from (measured against the
  frames labelled with the `empty` answer).
- A `Watcher` asks the teacher only when it is worth it. It looks at the newest frame, one at a time. It labels the
  frames it is sure about.
- Answers graduate the same way proxy questions do, except one answer at a time, because new answers keep appearing.
  Whenever the truth for a frame comes in (a confident look from the teacher, or a label from a person), the system
  checks the sure answer of the student against it. An answer graduates when the 95% lower bound on its agreement
  reaches `target` (0.9). This takes at least 20 checks, at most one per second, so in practice about 35 clean ones.
  If the upper bound drops below the target, the answer is demoted. `ask()` tells you if an answer has graduated.
  `report()` shows the checks and bounds for every answer.
- Until an answer graduates, the `Watcher` looks at it whenever it can. After that, it spot-checks the answer at
  random times, about every 10 seconds.
- An `Album` saves labelled frames (images or text) to disk, so they can be taught again after a restart.
- If you work with text and already have a teacher, use the proxy instead. It reads layer 8 and waits for a question
  to graduate before it answers locally. It audits, and it forwards anything it is not sure about. `hunch.live`
  always answers. This is correct when someone watches the stream and teaches it.

[`examples/objects`](../examples/objects/) and [`examples/gestures`](../examples/gestures/) are built on it, and the
module's docstring has the details.

[`web/live.ts`](web/live.ts) is the same `Choice`, `Detector` and `Watcher` in TypeScript, with `Eyes` running EG2's
