# Designing questions hunch can take over

Some questions can be learned by hunch's students and some can't. This guide lists what makes the difference, from
the examples, and gives a check to run before deploying a question. [../hunch/README.md](../hunch/README.md) explains
how hunch works; this page assumes you know what a teacher, a student and graduation are.

Terms used below:
- A **unit** is the text a question is asked about, such as one tool call and its output. hunch calls it a *state*;
  eg2cpu's compiled decisions call it a *unit*.
- **kappa** and **QWK** (quadratic weighted kappa, for ordered levels) measure agreement beyond chance: 1 is perfect,
  0 is chance. **AUC** measures how well scores rank the "yes" cases above the "no" cases: 1 is perfect, 0.5 random.
- A **hard negative** is an example that looks like a "yes" but isn't, such as source code that mentions an error.
- **Symmetric** and **one-sided** are hunch's two graduation modes: a symmetric student answers every question it is
  confident about; a one-sided one answers only a confident "no" and passes every possible "yes" to the teacher.

The evidence comes from these examples, all in [../examples](../examples): `proxy_replay` (hunch's policy against a
teacher on 2,000 tool results from public coding-agent sessions), `pii`, `prompt_injection`, `injection_teacher`,
`failure_severity` and `levels_sst5`.

## What limits a question

| limit | evidence | why |
|---|---|---|
| **The answer must be readable in the unit's text** | Output kind: kappa 0.94 against the teacher. PII present: AUC 0.97 for a probe trained on labelled gretel windows (layer 8, held out by document type), 0.88 for the decision compiled from 200 contrasts. Sentiment intensity: QWK 0.63 (the spec) to 0.70 (`layer: auto`). Failure severity: QWK 0.45 | Embeddings encode what the text says. "Who can fix this?", "what did the user want?" and "is the world in this state?" need context or reasoning. |
| **Topic vs property** | Code that *mentions* errors read as failures (26% correct without hard negatives); PII field names scored like PII values | The encoder reads what the text is about. Without matched contrasts and hard negatives, a question about a property gets answered about the topic. |
| **Rare answers** | `tool_failed` (5% "yes") never graduates symmetrically: recall on "yes" caps at about 0.75. One-sided, it answers about 70% locally, all of it "no", so its agreement with the teacher (0.995) only matches always answering "no". Blocking errors (about 1 in 80) are never learnable | A few positives can't prove recall, and agreement is fooled by base rates: always answering "no" agrees 95% of the time. |
| **Teacher blind spots** | The teacher catches 20% of polite prompt injections. On the same 26 held-out ones (unseen tools, attacks and fillers) it catches 23%, a student trained on its answers 27%, and the same student trained on ground truth 81% | A student copies its teacher's misses. It can't be better than its teacher unless it learns from something else. |
| **Teacher consistency** | The teacher calls 20% of harness-flagged errors "not failed", and is unsure on 35% of severity answers | The student copies the teacher, so an inconsistent teacher sets the ceiling. |
| **Format shift** | Prompt injection: the compiled decision reaches AUC 0.999 on familiar tool formats but 0.90 on new ones, where it flags 37% of imperative benign texts; a student trained on 200 InjecAgent labels flags 47% of real coding-agent tool outputs | Students learn format cues. Novelty checks and audits catch this, at the cost of coverage. |
| **Scales** | Sentiment levels worked; severity levels didn't (held-out levels came out of order) | A scale works when the wording intensifies along it, not when its levels are causal categories. |
| **Whether vs where** | Detecting takes one encoder pass; locating the part of the text responsible takes about 8 (re-encoding fragments) | An embedding of the whole text says whether, not where. |
| **Bundled questions** | One ungraduated question in a request sent every request to the teacher | The teacher reads the state once for all questions, so forwarding part of a request saves little. |
| **Unit length** | The encoder reads at most 1,024 tokens, and a small signal dilutes in a long unit | hunch keeps the head and tail of a long state; otherwise, split long outputs yourself or leave them to the teacher. |
| **Layer** | The compiled `tool_call_failed` direction is best at layer 20 on real traces (AUC 0.92), with the final embedding level with it (0.90) and layers 12 and 23 worst; PII reads best at the final layer on gretel | Questions live in different layers. hunch reads one layer for every question (`--layer`, default 8); the pre-flight shows which layer each question needs. |

## Rules for writing questions

1. **Ask about a unit, not the trace.** Ask "Did this tool call fail?" of each tool result, not "Did the agent
   struggle?" of the trace. Build trace-level answers in code from unit-level ones. Every success above was at the
   unit level.
2. **Ask for observable properties, and compose judgements in code.** Don't ask "How severe is this failure?". Ask
   "did it fail?" (the harness already knows), "does it mention credentials, permissions, quotas or rate limits?" and
   "is it an empty result?", then let a short program assign severity. Each sub-question is readable from the text;
   the judgement lives in code, where it's transparent and free.
3. **Put the rare answer on the "yes" side, and keep it binary.** Ask "Contains a secret?" or "Blocked by something
   outside the agent's reach?". Rare yes/no questions graduate one-sided. Split a rare class out of a multi-class
   question into its own yes/no question, rather than hoping a 2% class survives a 7-way choice.
4. **Use a scale (`score`) only for intensity.** "How frustrated is the user?" fits. "Which kind of failure?" is a
   `choice`.
5. **Say what doesn't count.** For example: "Source code or docs that mention errors are not a failure"; "naming a
   field without its value is not PII". This makes the teacher more consistent, and the teacher's answers are what
   the student learns. If you also use eg2cpu's compiled decisions, add the same cases to them as hard negatives.
6. **Freeze the wording, and name the family.** Graduation and the teacher's answers belong to the exact question
   text, and rewording starts over. Give every question a `family`, so its labelled examples survive a rewording.
   Change the wording deliberately: test the new wording on a dev set and a test set first, as `../examples/question_pilot/`
   does. Ask one general question of every tool, with the tool named in the state, rather than one hand-worded
   question per tool.
7. **Give the unit what the question needs, and nothing more.** Include the call with its output, and keep units
   short. Known facts (exit code, harness flag, tool name) can be extra fields of the state: hunch adds them to the
   text it reads, as `name: value` lines, and your code can use them directly.
8. **Group questions by how well they graduate.** Put questions that graduate, or are likely to, in their own
   requests. Don't bundle a severity or world-state question with them, or every request pays for the teacher.
9. **Check the teacher before learning from it.** Where some ground truth exists (benchmarks, harness flags,
   labelled samples), run the pre-flight twice, once on the teacher's answers and once on the ground truth, and score
   the teacher against the ground truth. If the teacher has a blind spot, train the student on the ground truth
   (`labelled` cases), and keep the teacher for what the student passes on.
10. **Route safety questions one-sided.** For injections, secrets and destructive actions, a miss costs more than a
    forward: prefer one-sided graduation even when symmetric passes.

## What phrasing can't fix

Some questions need reasoning or knowledge the unit doesn't contain: precondi

1	# hunch
2	
3	hunch is a proxy: it sits in front of a /v1/systemone model you might already be using to answer questions about textual data (like
4	"did this tool call fail in this agent trace?", "is this log entry from a hacker?"). It learns to answer the easy questions itself, but way faster,
5	making your whole system more responsive (and sometimes smarter too!).
6	
7	- **The teacher** either an LLM judge or a dedicated decision model. This is what hunch learns from.
8	- **The student** is hunch's own classifier model, one per question: Once cross-validation on the teacher's answers
9	  shows the student agrees with the teacher often enough, the question *graduates* and the student answers it.
10	- **A state** what we ask questions about: e.g. a tool call and its output, a message (or really any JSON).
11	
12	A question has a type:
13	- `noul`: yes or no (the question protocol's name for it), answered as P(yes);
14	- `choice`: one of named options, given as `criteria` (option name -> description);
15	- `score`: one of ordered levels, given as `criteria` (a list, lowest first).
16	
17	## Quick start
18	
19	```bash
20	python -m hunch serve --db proxy.db --backend http://teacher.example/v1/answer   # listens on 127.0.0.1:8765
21	```
22	
23	```bash
24	curl -s localhost:8765/v1/answer -d '{"state": {"call": "bash: ls config/", "output": "ls: config/: No such file or directory"},
25	  "questions": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the tool call fail?"}}}'
26	```
27	
28	```json
29	{"answers": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.97, "answered_by": "backend"}}, "answered_by": "backend", "model": "teacher"}
30	```
31	
32	`answered_by` lets you know who got it: `backend` (the teacher), `proxy` (the student) or `cache` (previously answered, reused).
33	
34	A question with options looks like this:
35	
36	```json
37	{"type": "choice", "instructions": "What kind of output is this?",
38	 "criteria": {"test_run": "Output of running tests", "build": "Output of a build or compile", "other": "Anything else"}}
39	```
40	
41	## The teacher
42	
43	hunch sends a `POST` request to the teacher, `{"state": ..., "questions": {id: question}}`, and expects
44	`{"answers": {id: answer}}` back, with an answer for every question:
45	- `noul`: `{"type": "noul", "noul": 0.97}`, P(yes);
46	- `choice`: `{"type": "choice", "probabilities": {"test_run": 0.9, "build": 0.05, "other": 0.05}}`;
47	- `score`: `{"type": "score", "probabilities": {"0": 0.1, "1": 0.7, "2": 0.2}}`, by level index.
48	
49	hunch's returns the same response, plus `choice` or `score` and `confidence` fields.
50	
51	 - `--backend`: is the teacher's URL. 
52	 - `--backend-header 'Authorization: Bearer …'`: adds headers to the teacher's requests, and
53	 - `--backend-timeout` (default 30 s) sets a timout.
54	
55	Teacher problems turn into a 502 for the caller: an error, a timeout, a missing question or an answer hunch can't
56	parse.
57	
58	## How it decides
59	
60	For each request, in order:
61	1. **The store.** If the store already holds an answer for this exact state and every question, hunch returns it. The
62	   answer is a label or the teacher's last answer.
63	2. **The students.** The students answer if all of these are true: every question has graduated, its student is
64	   confident, and the state is not novel. A novel state is unlike the examples the student learned from.
65	3. **The teacher.** Otherwise the whole request goes to the teacher. The teacher reads the state once for all
66	   questions. Every answer becomes a training example.
67	
68	The store is read by the hash of the state's text, so a stored answer needs no encoding. And when a question in the
69	request hasn't graduated, or is demoted, the request is bound for the teacher whatever its features say: hunch asks
70	the teacher at once and encodes the state at the same time, for learning and audits. Until a question graduates, a
71	request then takes as long as the slower of the two, not both one after the other.
72	
73	**Graduation.** A refit retrains a question's student and cross-validates it on its examples. The question
74	graduates in one of two modes:
75	- **symmetric:** on the states it is confident enough to answer, the student agrees with the teacher at least 90% of
76	  the time, and on at least 80% of the answers other than the most common one (both the 95% lower bound);
77	- **one-sided** (`noul` only): the student answers only when it is confident the answer is "no", and passes every
78	  likely "yes" to the teacher. This needs at most 2% of its "no" answers to be wrong, and at least 85% of the teacher's
79	  "yes" answers to be passed on. It suits rare, important answers, such as "is this an injection?".
80	
81	A question refits on a worker thread once it has 100 new examples (`--refit-every`). The system checks the count each
82	time it records the answers of the teacher. Requests keep the previous fit until the new fit is swapped in. `train`
83	with `"refit": true` (the default) refits before it responds. With `"refit": false`, its examples count toward the
84	next check. The refit then waits for the next answer from the teacher. The refits of one question run one at a time.
85	The fit in use is therefore always from the newest examples. Fits are kept in the store, so a restarted proxy answers
86	at once.
87	
88	**Audits.** Graduated questions keep being checked against the teacher:
89	- 10% of the students' answers (`--audit`) are also sent to the teacher, in the background: the client gets the
90	  student's answer without waiting. If the teacher is down, the audit fails, not the request.
91	- Every request that goes to the teacher anyway also checks each student that would have answered it.
92	
93	A question is demoted while its last 100 audits are significantly below its bar. The bar is: agreement below 90%
94	(symmetric), or more than 2% of "no" answers wrong (one-sided). While a question is demoted, its requests go to the
95	teacher. The question answers again when its audits recover. The store keeps the audits, so a demoted question stays
96	demoted after a restart. A refit that changes its mode starts a new window, because the old audits measured the other
97	mode. The thresholds and their statistics are in [../docs/glossary.md](../docs/glossary.md#the-proxy-hunch).
98	
99	Which questions can graduate at all is the subject of [../docs/question-design.md](../docs/question-design.md).
100	
101	## Training: `POST /v1/train`
102	
103	You can also give hunch answers directly:
104	
105	```json
106	{"question": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "Did the tool call fail?"},
107	 "cases": [
108	   {"state": {"call": "bash: ls config/", "output": "ls: config/: No such file or directory"}, "answer": true, "kind": "labelled"},
109	   {"state": "added 214 packages in 6s", "answer": {"type": "noul", "noul": 0.04}, "kind": "sampled"}],
110	 "refit": true}
111	```
112	
113	- **`sampled`** answers are treated as the teacher's, for example answers collected from its logs. hunch keeps the
114	  newest 2,000 per question (`--sampled-cap`), together with the answers it forwards, and weights each by its
115	  confidence.
116	- **`labelled`** answers are ground truth: benchmark labels, harness flags, human review. hunch keeps the newest
117	  5,000 of each class per family (`--labelled-cap`); they weigh twice as much as a sampled answer, and win over a
118	  sampled answer for the same state. They are how a student learns
119	  past a teacher's blind spot (`../examples/injection_teacher/`).
120	- **`answer`** can be a label (`true`/`"yes"`/`1` for `noul`, an option name for `choice`, a level index or legend
121	  entry for `score`), P(yes) as a bare number for `noul` (`0.04`), a list of probabilities in option order
122	  (`[p_yes]` for `noul`), or an answer object. Probabilities must be in [0, 1]; a request with any invalid answer
123	  gets 400, and none of its cases are kept.
124	
125	Each state counts once per question. A new answer for a state replaces the old answer. The response is the status of
126	the question after the refit.
127	
128	For each labelled state, hunch also keeps the teacher's answer. This lets hunch measure the teacher against ground
129	truth. If the teacher has already answered the state, hunch keeps that answer. If not, hunch asks the teacher in the
130	background. It makes one call per state, which covers every version of the question it knows. `--no-ask-for-labels`
131	turns those calls off. Answers that arrive later through traffic are still kept. The question's status reports how
132	many labels have a teacher answer (`labels_with_teacher`).
133	
134	### Teacher tuning
135	
136	Those pairs let hunch tune the teacher. An LLM judge often ranks well but puts its cut points in the wrong place. In
137	the examples, a judge that separated prompt injections with AUC 0.96 scored 0.62 accuracy at its default 0.5. At each
138	refit, a question version with at least 50 labels that have a teacher answer fits a recalibration of the teacher. The
139	recalibration is a logistic regression on the log-probabilities of the teacher, with each class weighted equally.
140	5-fold cross-validation then compares it with the raw teacher, answer by answer. Tuning switches on only if it
141	significantly improves balanced accuracy, which counts each class equally. It must also not significantly lower plain
142	accuracy. The balanced test stops the tuning from winning by never predicting a rare class. The plain test stops a
143	class seen only a few times from carrying the tuning.
144	
145	When tuning is on, every answer from the teacher is recalibrated. This includes an answer that was just forwarded and
146	an answer replayed from the store. The original answer of the teacher stays under `untuned`. To see whether tuning is
147	on, and why, read the status of the question under `report.tuning`.
148	
149	Students then aim at the tuned answers, in two tiers. At each refit, hunch fits two students:
150	- **Full:** Learns the answers of the tuned teacher. Once it graduates, it answers.
151	- **Partial:** Learns the own answers of the teacher, but is graded against the tuned answers. It answers only until
152	  the full student graduates.
153	
154	Grading the partial student against tuned answers keeps it to the states where tuning didn't change the answer.
155	Those are usually most of them: clear successes and clear failures, far from either cut point. States near the
156	moved cut point go to the teacher.
157	
158	Audits compare against the tuned answer. Every local answer says which tier answered (`tier`). The question's status
159	does the same.
160	
161	Tuning only moves the cut points. It does not make the teacher see things it misses. A student trained on labels with
162	the features of EG2 can learn past a blind spot. A recalibrated teacher cannot.
163	
164	### Blind spots
165	
166	`GET /v1/questions/{key}/blind_spots` (or `proxy.blind_spots(question)`) shows where the teacher disagrees with your
167	labels. It uses the tuned teacher when tuning is on. It reads only what the store already has, so it makes no teacher
168	calls:
169	- **Summary:** the accuracy of the teacher on the labels, raw and as served, a confusion matrix of label against the
170	  answer of the teacher, and recall for each label. A label that the teacher never predicts shows up here.
171	- **Spots:** the disagreements, grouped by (label, answer of the teacher) and clustered by EG2 features. The largest
172	  and most confidently wrong are first. Each spot gives its size, the probability of the teacher for the label, and
173	  the share where an out-of-fold student agrees with the label. A high share suggests a real blind spot. A low share
174	  suggests label noise, or a question that the labels and the teacher read differently.
175	- **What to label next:** for each spot, the number of unlabelled states from traffic that the teacher answered the
176	  same way within the radius of the spot, and the nearest few. They show whether a spot is a handful of cases or a
177	  large part of your traffic.
178	
179	States come with their text when hunch keeps texts (`--store-text`). Otherwise, they come as hashes. The endpoint can
180	return stored texts. So it needs the training token when a token is set.
181	
182	On the pi stream, the largest spot is searches that find nothing. The stream uses Clef's severity answers, 400 of our
183	labels, and the other 1,600 results as traffic. The rubric calls these searches minor. Clef calls them none. Several
184	hundred traffic results look alike. That is a wording problem, not a model problem. The clearest true blind spot is
185	GitHub issue text that describes errors. Clef reads it as a failure. The student backs the labels that say it is not
186	a failure.
187	
188	## Rewording questions: versions and families
189	
190	A question's *version* is its type, instructions and criteria, so a reworded question is a new version: it starts with
191	no sampled answers and no graduation, because the teacher's answers to one wording aren't answers to another. To keep
192	ground truth across rewordings, name the question's family:
193	
194	```json
195	{"type": "noul", "family": "injection", "instructions": "…reworded…"}
196	```
197	
198	- Every version in a family uses the labelled examples of the family. A new wording can therefore graduate before it
199	  has seen a single teacher answer.
200	- A version trained without a family joins one, with its labels, the first time a question names it.
201	- Versions in a family must have the same type and options. Otherwise their labels mean different things.
202	- A request may leave the family out once a version is known.
203	
204	## Running it
205	
206	| endpoint | |
207	|---|---|
208	| `POST /v1/answer` | a request (above) |
209	| `POST /v1/train` | training cases (above) |
210	| `GET /v1/questions` | `{"ready", "stats", "latency", "layer", "encoder", "states", "questions": [...]}`: request counts, latency by who answered, and each question's examples, graduation, cross-validation report and audits |
211	| `GET /healthz` | 200 while the process is up |
212	| `GET /readyz` | 200 once every question restored from the store has a fit, else 503 |
213	
214	- **Access:** `--token` (or `$HUNCH_TOKEN`) makes every endpoint but `/healthz` and `/readyz` require
215	  `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. `--train-token` (or `$HUNCH_TRAIN_TOKEN`) gives `/v1/train` its own token, since
216	  training writes ground truth. Without a token the server is open, so keep it on `127.0.0.1` (the default `--host`).
217	- **Limits:** request bodies over `--max-body` (1 MiB) get 413, and a POST without a valid `Content-Length` gets 411
218	  or 400; the token is checked before the body is read. A client that sends nothing for `--client-timeout` seconds
219	  (30), idle or mid-request, is disconnected. At most `--max-connections` (64) connections are served at once, each
220	  on its own thread; one more gets 503.
221	- **Errors:** an unexpected failure gets 500 with only an `error_id`; the detail is logged to stderr under that id.
222	- **CPU:** `--threads` caps the threads the encoder uses (the default is every core).
223	- **Logs:** `--access-log` writes one line per request to stderr: method, path, status, milliseconds, who answered.
224	
225	**Storage.** `--db` takes a SQLite path, or a Redis URL (`redis://host:port/db?prefix=name`, with
226	`pip install hunch[redis]`). The store holds:
227	- each state once, by the hash of its text: its layer-8 features (2 KB) and, with `--store-text`, the text;
228	- each question's examples (one per state), its latest fit and its last 100 audits;
229	- the encoder fingerprint: the checkpoint revision, layer, matmul precision and clipping that computed the features.
230	  A proxy with a different encoder refuses the store; with `--store-text`, `--rebuild` re-encodes the stored states
231	  and refits every question on the new features.
232	
233	Several processes can share a Redis store, but each keeps its own students and refit counters. They share examples,
234	fits and the audits they record. Each process reads the audits only when it starts, so their demotions can differ.
235	
236	**State text.** The encoder and the teacher read a state as its text: a tool call and its output as `call\noutput`,
237	followed by any other fields as `name: value` lines, and any other JSON as sorted JSON. The encoder reads at most 1,024
238	tokens, so a state over 3,000 characters is clipped to its head and tail, keeping the end of a long output, where an
239	error usually is.
240	
241	## Performance
242	
243	Measured on an Apple M5 Pro with the real encoder, on real tool results of about 190 tokens (one question per
244	request, the teacher replayed with a 500 ms delay):
245	
246	| | p50 | p95 | p99 |
247	|---|---|---|---|
248	| answered by the student, one request at a time | 22 ms | 51 ms | 76 ms |
249	| answered by the teacher | 531 ms | 579 ms | 583 ms |
250	
251	Audited answers return as fast as other student answers. The audit happens afterwards.
252	
253	Concurrent requests share the encoder: one thread encodes whatever is waiting as one batch. Throughput rises with load,
254	and latency under load is mostly the wait for the current batch:
255	
256	| concurrent callers | requests/s | p50 | p95 | p99 |
257	|---|---|---|---|---|
258	| 1 | 41 | 21 ms | 47 ms | 71 ms |
259	| 4 | 51 | 83 ms | 122 ms | 137 ms |
260	| 16 | 73 | 226 ms | 294 ms | 301 ms |
261	| 32 | 86 | 382 ms | 451 ms | 466 ms |
262	
263	- **CPU and memory:** a single caller keeps about 7 cores busy while a request is encoded. `--threads` caps that. The
264	  process holds about 1.5 GB, the model included.
265	- **Restart:** a restarted proxy is ready at once. It answers from the kept fits.
266	- **Cost per request** is mostly the encoder pass to layer 8. It grows with the length of the state, up to the
267	  1,024-token limit. The encoder's own numbers, batched and per hardware, are in
268	  [../docs/performance.md](../docs/performance.md).
269	
270	## From Python
271	
272	```python
273	from hunch import HTTPBackend, Proxy
274	
275	proxy = Proxy(backend=HTTPBackend("http://teacher.example/v1/answer"), db="proxy.db")
276	proxy.answer({"state": {"call": "...", "output": "..."}, "questions": {"failed": {"type": "noul", "instructions": "..."}}})
277	proxy.train(question, cases)       # as POST /v1/train
278	proxy.predict(question, states)    # the student's answers for many states, without routing or learning
279	proxy.wait()                       # until pending refits and background audits are done
280	```
281	
282	Custom stores implement `hunch.Store`.
283	
284	## Live images: `hunch.live`
285	
286	The proxy answers questions about text states behind a teacher. `hunch.live` answers questions about a stream, from
287	one EG2 embedding per item. It learns from the items that a person or a teacher labels as it runs. An item is an
288	image or a text. An image is, for example, a webcam frame (about 110 ms on an Apple M5 Pro's CPU at 70 soft tokens).
289	A text takes about 12 ms for a short tool result, by the full pass, so it shares the space of the prompts.
290	
291	```python
292	from hunch.live import Choice, Detector, Eyes, Watcher
293	
294	eyes = Eyes(tokens=70)
295	seen = Choice(eyes, {"nothing": ["a person with empty hands"], "mug": ["a person holding up a mug"]},
296	              quiet={"nothing"}, empty="nothing", new=lambda name: [f"a person holding up a {name}"])
297	fire = Detector(eyes, yes=["a photo of fire"], no=["a normal indoor photo"], threshold=-0.04)
298	
299	x, ms = eyes.see(jpeg)            # or eyes.see("bash('npm test') -> 'Error: Timeout of 2000ms exceeded'")
300	seen.ask(x)                     # {"name", "p", "state": quiet | sure | unsure, "probs", "zero", ...}
301	seen.teach(x, "seashell")       # a new answer, with new("seashell")'s prompts; the student refits in the background
302	seen.forget()                   # back to the answers it started with
303	watcher = Watcher(seen, teacher)  # teacher(jpeg, names) -> {name or hunch.live.ELSE: probability}
304	watcher.look(jpeg, x, seen.ask(x))
305	```
306	
307	- Every answer starts out zero-shot, from its text prompts. When you label frames, a logistic regression learns from
308	  them. The trust in it depends on how much a new frame looks like the frames it learned from (measured against the
309	  frames labelled with the `empty` answer).
310	- A `Watcher` asks the teacher only when it is worth it. It looks at the newest frame, one at a time. It labels the
311	  frames it is sure about.
312	- Answers graduate the same way proxy questions do, except one answer at a time, because new answers keep appearing.
313	  Whenever the truth for a frame comes in (a confident look from the teacher, or a label from a person), the system
314	  checks the sure answer of the student against it. An answer graduates when the 95% lower bound on its agreement
315	  reaches `target` (0.9). This takes at least 20 checks, at most one per second, so in practice about 35 clean ones.
316	  If the upper bound drops below the target, the answer is demoted. `ask()` tells you if an answer has graduated.
317	  `report()` shows the checks and bounds for every answer.
318	- Until an answer graduates, the `Watcher` looks at it whenever it can. After that, it spot-checks the answer at
319	  random times, about every 10 seconds.
320	- An `Album` saves labelled frames (images or text) to disk, so they can be taught again after a restart.
321	- If you work with text and already have a teacher, use the proxy instead. It reads layer 8 and waits for a question
322	  to graduate before it answers locally. It audits, and it forwards anything it is not sure about. `hunch.live`
323	  always answers. This is correct when someone watches the stream and teaches it.
324	
325	[`examples/objects`](../examples/objects/) and [`examples/gestures`](../examples/gestures/) are built on it, and the
326	module's docstring has the details.
327	
328	### In the browser
329	
330	[`web/live.ts`](web/live.ts) is the same `Choice`, `Detector` and `Watcher` in TypeScript, with `Eyes` running EG2's
331	image path on the GPU through WebGPU ([`web/eg2/`](web/eg2/), about 60 ms a frame on an Apple M5 Pro in Chrome). The
332	browser runs no text path, so prompts arrive as vectors embedded beforehand with eg2cpu. `web/dist/live.js` is the
333	bundle; `npm run build` in `web/` makes it again, and `npm run check` type-checks.
334	
335	```js
336	import { Choice, Eyes } from './hunch/web/dist/live.js';
337	
338	const eyes = await Eyes.open({ weights: 'weights', tokens: 70 });   // examples/browser/convert.py writes the weights
339	const things = new Choice({ nothing: nothingVector, mug: mugVector }, { quiet: ['nothing'], empty: 'nothing' });
340	const { x, ms } = await eyes.see(video);
341	things.ask(x); things.teach(x, 'seashell'); things.forget();
342	```
343	
344	[`examples/browser`](../examples/browser/) is built on it.
345	
346	## Tests
347	
348	```bash
349	uv run --package hunch pytest -q hunch/tests
350	```
351	
352	The tests use a fake encoder, so they don't need the model.
353	# Designing questions hunch can take over
354	
355	Some questions can be learned by hunch's students and some can't. This guide lists what makes the difference, from
356	the examples, and gives a check to run before deploying a question. [../hunch/README.md](../hunch/README.md) explains
357	how hunch works; this page assumes you know what a teacher, a student and graduation are.
358	
359	Terms used below:
360	- A **unit** is the text a question is asked about, such as one tool call and its output. hunch calls it a *state*;
361	  eg2cpu's compiled decisions call it a *unit*.
362	- **kappa** and **QWK** (quadratic weighted kappa, for ordered levels) measure agreement beyond chance: 1 is perfect,
363	  0 is chance. **AUC** measures how well scores rank the "yes" cases above the "no" cases: 1 is perfect, 0.5 random.
364	- A **hard negative** is an example that looks like a "yes" but isn't, such as source code that mentions an error.
365	- **Symmetric** and **one-sided** are hunch's two graduation modes: a symmetric student answers every question it is
366	  confident about; a one-sided one answers only a confident "no" and passes every possible "yes" to the teacher.
367	
368	The evidence comes from these examples, all in [../examples](../examples): `proxy_replay` (hunch's policy against a
369	teacher on 2,000 tool results from public coding-agent sessions), `pii`, `prompt_injection`, `injection_teacher`,
370	`failure_severity` and `levels_sst5`.
371	
372	## What limits a question
373	
374	| limit | evidence | why |
375	|---|---|---|
376	| **The answer must be readable in the unit's text** | Output kind: kappa 0.94 against the teacher. PII present: AUC 0.97 for a probe trained on labelled gretel windows (layer 8, held out by document type), 0.88 for the decision compiled from 200 contrasts. Sentiment intensity: QWK 0.63 (the spec) to 0.70 (`layer: auto`). Failure severity: QWK 0.45 | Embeddings encode what the text says. "Who can fix this?", "what did the user want?" and "is the world in this state?" need context or reasoning. |
377	| **Topic vs property** | Code that *mentions* errors read as failures (26% correct without hard negatives); PII field names scored like PII values | The encoder reads what the text is about. Without matched contrasts and hard negatives, a question about a property gets answered about the topic. |
378	| **Rare answers** | `tool_failed` (5% "yes") never graduates symmetrically: recall on "yes" caps at about 0.75. One-sided, it answers about 70% locally, all of it "no", so its agreement with the teacher (0.995) only matches always answering "no". Blocking errors (about 1 in 80) are never learnable | A few positives can't prove recall, and agreement is fooled by base rates: always answering "no" agrees 95% of the time. |
379	| **Teacher blind spots** | The teacher catches 20% of polite prompt injections. On the same 26 held-out ones (unseen tools, attacks and fillers) it catches 23%, a student trained on its answers 27%, and the same student trained on ground truth 81% | A student copies its teacher's misses. It can't be better than its teacher unless it learns from something else. |
380	| **Teacher consistency** | The teacher calls 20% of harness-flagged errors "not failed", and is unsure on 35% of severity answers | The student copies the teacher, so an inconsistent teacher sets the ceiling. |
381	| **Format shift** | Prompt injection: the compiled decision reaches AUC 0.999 on familiar tool formats but 0.90 on new ones, where it flags 37% of imperative benign texts; a student trained on 200 InjecAgent labels flags 47% of real coding-agent tool outputs | Students learn format cues. Novelty checks and audits catch this, at the cost of coverage. |
382	| **Scales** | Sentiment levels worked; severity levels didn't (held-out levels came out of order) | A scale works when the wording intensifies along it, not when its levels are causal categories. |
383	| **Whether vs where** | Detecting takes one encoder pass; locating the part of the text responsible takes about 8 (re-encoding fragments) | An embedding of the whole text says whether, not where. |
384	| **Bundled questions** | One ungraduated question in a request sent every request to the teacher | The teacher reads the state once for all questions, so forwarding part of a request saves little. |
385	| **Unit length** | The encoder reads at most 1,024 tokens, and a small signal dilutes in a long unit | hunch keeps the head and tail of a long state; otherwise, split long outputs yourself or leave them to the teacher. |
386	| **Layer** | The compiled `tool_call_failed` direction is best at layer 20 on real traces (AUC 0.92), with the final embedding level with it (0.90) and layers 12 and 23 worst; PII reads best at the final layer on gretel | Questions live in different layers. hunch reads one layer for every question (`--layer`, default 8); the pre-flight shows which layer each question needs. |
387	
388	## Rules for writing questions
389	
390	1. **Ask about a unit, not the trace.** Ask "Did this tool call fail?" of each tool result, not "Did the agent
391	   struggle?" of the trace. Build trace-level answers in code from unit-level ones. Every success above was at the
392	   unit level.
393	2. **Ask for observable properties, and compose judgements in code.** Don't ask "How severe is this failure?". Ask
394	   "did it fail?" (the harness already knows), "does it mention credentials, permissions, quotas or rate limits?" and
395	   "is it an empty result?", then let a short program assign severity. Each sub-question is readable from the text;
396	   the judgement lives in code, where it's transparent and free.
397	3. **Put the rare answer on the "yes" side, and keep it binary.** Ask "Contains a secret?" or "Blocked by something
398	   outside the agent's reach?". Rare yes/no questions graduate one-sided. Split a rare class out of a multi-class
399	   question into its own yes/no question, rather than hoping a 2% class survives a 7-way choice.
400	4. **Use a scale (`score`) only for intensity.** "How frustrated is the user?" fits. "Which kind of failure?" is a
401	   `choice`.
402	5. **Say what doesn't count.** For example: "Source code or docs that mention errors are not a failure"; "naming a
403	   field without its value is not PII". This makes the teacher more consistent, and the teacher's answers are what
404	   the student learns. If you also use eg2cpu's compiled decisions, add the same cases to them as hard negatives.
405	6. **Freeze the wording, and name the family.** Graduation and the teacher's answers belong to the exact question
406	   text, and rewording starts over. Give every question a `family`, so its labelled examples survive a rewording.
407	   Change the wording deliberately: test the new wording on a dev set and a test set first, as `../examples/question_pilot/`
408	   does. Ask one general question of every tool, with the tool named in the state, rather than one hand-worded
409	   question per tool.
410	7. **Give the unit what the question needs, and nothing more.** Include the call with its output, and keep units
411	   short. Known facts (exit code, harness flag, tool name) can be extra fields of the state: hunch adds them to the
412	   text it reads, as `name: value` lines, and your code can use them directly.
413	8. **Group questions by how well they graduate.** Put questions that graduate, or are likely to, in their own
414	   requests. Don't bundle a severity or world-state question with them, or every request pays for the teacher.
415	9. **Check the teacher before learning from it.** Where some ground truth exists (benchmarks, harness flags,
416	   labelled samples), run the pre-flight twice, once on the teacher's answers and once on the ground truth, and score
417	   the teacher against the ground truth. If the teacher has a blind spot, train the student on the ground truth
418	   (`labelled` cases), and keep the teacher for what the student passes on.
419	10. **Route safety questions one-sided.** For injections, secrets and destructive actions, a miss costs more than a
420	    forward: prefer one-sided graduation even when symmetric passes.
421	
422	## What phrasing can't fix
423	
424	Some questions need reasoning or knowledge the unit doesn't contain: preconditions, causal severity, "should the
425	agent have done X?". Those stay with the teacher however they're worded. hunch finds this out itself: those questions
426	never graduate, and audits keep the ones that did graduate honest.
427	
428	## Pre-flight check
429	
430	Collect 150–300 teacher answers on real units, and from `examples/` run the check before deploying a question:
431	
432	```bash
433	uv run preflight/preflight.py answers.jsonl --type noul --name tool_failed
434	```
435	
436	```bash
437	uv run preflight/preflight.py answers.jsonl --type choice --options source,test_run,build,search,vcs,edit,other
438	```
439	
440	```bash
441	uv run preflight/preflight.py answers.jsonl --type score --options none,minor,recoverable,blocking
442	```
443	
444	**Input.** `answers.jsonl` has one line per unit (`span` is the unit, the state hunch would see):
445	
446	```json
447	{"span": {"call": "...", "output": "..."}, "answer": [0.03], "group": "<session id>"}
448	```
449	
450	- `answer` is the teacher's probabilities or a label. Each option has one probability. For `noul`, the probabilities
451	  are `[p_yes]`.
452	- `group` keeps the units of a session in the same cross-validation fold, as hunch meets them.
453	- `--hard hard.jsonl` adds units that must read a given answer.
454	
455	**What it does.** It cross-validates a student against the teacher for layers 4, 8 and 12 and the final embedding. It
456	uses the graduation rules of hunch ([glossary](glossary.md#the-proxy-hunch)). It costs each layer at its measured
457	encoding time on your units. For `score` questions, it also checks Spearman correlation, QWK, how often the answer is
458	within one level, and whether the levels come out in order. It reports how unsure the teacher is. It reports how many
459	units exceed the 1,024-token window. It ends with one verdict:
460	
461	| verdict | meaning | what to do |
462	|---|---|---|
463	| **GRADUATES symmetrically** at layer *k* | the expected coverage, kappa and cost per item | deploy, reading layer *k* |
464	| **GRADUATES ONE-SIDED** | only a confident "no" would be answered locally | deploy; hunch picks one-sided itself |
465	| **NOT ENOUGH DATA** | too few rare answers to prove recall; it prints how many more to collect, and the CV AUC (whether there is any signal) | collect more, re-run |
466	| **BACKEND ONLY** | no layer passes | rephrase (rules 1–5 and 7, with the printed hints), or keep the question on the teacher |
467	
468	**Does it predict the replay?** On the first 300 units of the shipped stream, the check gave the same verdicts as the
469	full 2,000-unit replays. Costs are estimated compute per unit, compared with the teacher's 494 ms:
470	
471	| question | pre-flight on 300 units | replay on 2,000 |
472	|---|---|---|
473	| output_kind | graduates at layer 8: about 90% local, kappa 0.85, about 115 ms per unit | graduated at unit 149; 92% local at layer 8, kappa 0.94 |
474	| tool_failed | not enough data: 16 "yes" answers where about 33 are needed (CV AUC 0.79) | graduated one-sided at unit 549 (lost it at 701, back at 1001) |
475	| severity | backend only: rare levels missed, levels out of order, teacher unsure on 35% | never graduated |
476	
477	For `tool_failed`, the check asked for about 320 more units. At 650 units, it asked for about 90 more units.
478	
479	**Prompt injection** (`injection_teacher`, 700 units grouped by tool): on the teacher's answers the question
480	graduates at layer 8 (kappa 0.87), and on the ground truth at layer 4 (kappa 0.89). Only the check against ground
481	truth shows that a student of this teacher would inherit its 80% miss rate on polite injections, which is rule 9.
482	
483	The pre-flight is a snapshot. hunch re-checks graduation as answers arrive and audits after graduating, so a question
484	that passes the pre-flight can still be demoted when the traffic shifts.

I'm a researcher planning how to make Maester (open-source PowerShell tool that runs ~750 security configuration checks against a Microsoft 365 / Entra tenant and produces an HTML report: pass/fail per check, severity, user impact, effort, MITRE ATT&CK, CIS/CISA/NIST mappings, affected objects, trends across runs) produce far more insightful reporting. I need a research digest of the state of the art, with links. Today's date is 2026-11-05. Use WebSearch (load it with ToolSearch "select:WebSearch,WebFetch" first) and WebFetch. Be selective: about 15–25 sources, prefer primary vendor docs, papers and well-known practitioner posts.

Cover these topics, each with 3–6 bullet findings and source links:

1. **Attack paths / toxic combinations / exposure graphs**: how Wiz (Security Graph, toxic combinations), Microsoft Security Exposure Management (attack paths, critical asset management, choke points), Tenable Identity Exposure / XM Cyber, BloodHound / AzureHound / EntraHound, ROADtools model identity relationships and turn individual misconfigurations into prioritized paths. What data model and what scoring.
2. **Prioritisation beyond severity**: choke-point / blast-radius scoring, "critical assets", SSVC (CISA's Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization), EPSS-style likelihood, Microsoft Secure Score's weighting, business-context weighting. Which are applicable to configuration findings (not CVEs)?
3. **LLM-generated security reporting**: Microsoft Security Copilot (promptbooks, Entra/Intune agents, Conditional Access optimization agent), Microsoft Zero Trust Assessment's report, any vendor doing LLM executive summaries/narratives of posture, plus known failure modes (hallucination, grounding) and mitigations (grounded generation, citations to data, structured output).
4. **Personalised / persona-based reporting**: CISO vs admin vs auditor views; reports that ask the reader their goal (e.g. "preparing for audit", "after an incident", "first time hardening", "M&A due diligence") and re-rank; questionnaire-driven risk scoping (e.g. NIST CSF profiles / tiers, CIS Implementation Groups IG1/IG2/IG3, Essential Eight maturity levels) as a way to tailor.
5. **"System One" / fast decision models and embedding classifiers** for security data: distilling an LLM judge into a small classifier (e.g. undrgrnd-labs/hunch on GitHub, TypeSafe's Jev/Clef decision models), embedding-based classifiers for log/sign-in/audit triage, semantic clustering of findings, and where it is a fit for an offline/local tool that runs in a customer's PowerShell session (no data leaves the tenant).
6. **Local/offline AI in admin tools**: running small models on-device (ONNX Runtime, WebGPU in the browser, llama.cpp, Phi/Gemma small models, EmbeddingGemma), and privacy considerations for tenant data in reports; MCP servers for M365 data (e.g. Lokka, Microsoft's own MCP servers) and WebMCP for letting an AI agent operate a web page.
7. **Inferring tenant context from data**: approaches that infer an organisation's profile (size, industry, maturity, hybrid vs cloud-only, critical assets, break-glass accounts, privileged users) from configuration and directory data rather than asking.

Then give a closing section "Ideas most transferable to a configuration-assessment report" — 8–12 concrete ideas, each one line, ranked by value/effort.

Return under ~2,000 words. Facts with links; mark anything speculative. Do not write any files.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /Users/merill/.claude/plugins/cache/typesafe-ai/typesafe/0.6.2/skills/typesafe-ai

# Build with TypeSafe

TypeSafe's **Jev**, the first public **System One model**, answers typed questions about state your
application supplies. State is the text, images, and application data your code sends with a
request. Jev can answer a Choice among options, a Noul (the probability that a statement is true), a
Score on levels you describe, or a Box that locates something in an image. Each answer comes back as
typed data with calibrated probabilities, for your code to use.

The rest of this skill is guidance: patterns that tend to produce reliable integrations. None of it
is absolute. Models change, applications differ, and edge cases exist. When a situation calls for
something else, test the alternative and use your judgment.

## Judgments from Jev, decisions in code

Integrations tend to work best when Jev makes the judgments and code decides what to do with
them. Think of each decision as a **truth table**. Jev supplies the inputs, such as "Does the
customer sound frustrated?" or "Which product is the message about?". Code holds the logic that
maps those inputs to an action.

A question that asks Jev to make the decision, such as "Should this ticket be escalated?" or "What
should the agent do next?", usually means the question is at the wrong layer. Instead, break the
decision into the judgments it depends on, and write the decision itself in code, where it's
visible and testable. Writing out the table often shows gaps in the business logic too. A
combination of judgments with no defined outcome is a design question about the system, and it is
best settled in code.

## Live docs

The live docs are the source of truth for request syntax, SDKs, question types, limits, and current
model behavior. Read the relevant pages as part of the task.

- Start at the [documentation index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt). Append `.md` to a page
  path to get the page as Markdown, and resolve relative links against `https://docs.typesafe.ai`.
- Exact request and response schemas: the [OpenAPI spec](https://api.typesafe.ai/openapi.json) and
  the [HTTP API](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/api.md) page. For an SDK, see the
  [Python](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/python-sdk.md) or
  [JavaScript](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/js-sdk.md) page and the types in the installed package.
- Question types: [primitives](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/primitives.md) and each type's own page,
  [structured instructions and criteria](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/advanced.md), and
  [images](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/images.md).
- Models, context limits, and rate limits: [models](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/models.md). Known
  model weak spots and their workarounds are on the
  [jaggedness page](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/jaggedness.md).
- Architecture: [how to build with TypeSafe](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/how-to-build.md),
  [patterns](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/patterns.md), and
  [cookbooks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md). The cookbook closest to your use case is a
  good starting point for a new workflow.

If you can't reach the live docs, use the installed SDK's types or local docs, and tell the user
you did. Leave out details that depend on the version rather than guessing them.

## Workflow

1. **Start from the decision logic.** Begin with what the application will show, select, change,
   or hand off. Sketch the truth table or rules that decide it, and list the inputs they need.
   Inputs that need an understanding of language or images make good questions. Arithmetic, dates,
   exact lookups, and policy usually belong in code. Aim for every question to feed the table, and
   give every combination of answers an outcome, including the case where a Noul lands between your
   thresholds. If code alone can already make the decision reliably, tell the user.
2. **Keep all question wording in one place.** Questions, options, criteria, and thresholds are the
   parts of an integration people audit and edit most. Keeping them together in one module makes
   that easier. [Design the state](#design-the-state) and
   [Write the questions](#write-the-questions) describe what tends to work.
3. **Probe the live API**: send test requests as described in
   [Test with the live API](#test-with-the-live-api). Use representative cases, hard cases, and
   negative cases. Keep going until the application behaves as intended.
4. **Integrate.** A few habits help here. Expose or log the exact request payload. When a call to
   the API fails, surface it as an error, not as an answer; for example, don't treat a failed call
   as a "no". Keep API keys on the server.

If the user's request is open-ended, offer the few directions from [Cookbooks](#cookbooks) that
best serve their goal, and recommend one. If the request is concrete, build it.

## Design the state

A useful check for any question is the **human test**: could a smart person, shown only this state
and this question, answer quickly by intuition? When a question fails the test, the fix is usually
in the state, not in the wording.

- **Give what a person would look at.** That means who sent each message, the full thread rather
  than a truncated last line, names rather than raw IDs or @-mention markup, and the item the
  question is about rather than the whole catalogue. State facts your code already knows, such as
  "all messages in `replies` were sent after the refund was issued", rather than leaving the model
  to work them out again.
- **Supply facts the model may lack**, such as what an internal product name or codename refers
  to.
- **Ensure every field in the state is relevant.** Irrelevant detail clutters the context and
  reduces accuracy. A field added for one question can sway the answer to another, and the model
  can read an empty list as a signal.
- **Be mindful when truncating.** Truncate long strings only when you need to, and check that the
  cut doesn't remove context the questions need.
- **Structure with named fields.** JSON objects with descriptive keys work better than a string of
  serialized JSON. They also let a question refer to each part by its path. Stable names such as
  `candidates.refund_policy` are easier to refer to than array positions.
- **Consider leaving out what no person could judge**, such as an unreadable crop or a distinction
  experts dispute. The model's answer there tends to be noise, and code will treat that noise as
  signal.

## Write the questions

Break complex judgments or decisions into their parts, and combine the answers in code with
weighted sums, boolean logic, thresholds, or other heuristics to reach the final decision. For
example, rather than asking "Is this fraud?" or "Is this spam?", ask the set of atomic questions
about what might make something fraud or spam. Each question tends to work best when it asks for
**one judgment** that a person could make at a glance.

- **Ask the concrete, observable thing.** Aim for something a person could point to: "Is a SQL
  query built by string concatenation here?" rather than "Are there SQL injection risks?".
- **One judgment per question; beware the "or".** Two conditions joined by "or" or "and" usually
  work better as two questions. Likewise, a list of rules usually works better as one question per
  rule.
- **Anchor intent to the goal.** When the judgment is about what someone wants, it helps to name
  their goal: "Which of these files does the user want copied?" rather than "Which of these names
  the main input?".
- **Name the subject directly.** "Where is the coffee mug in `photo`?" reads better than "Where is
  `target` in `photo`?" with the target defined somewhere else. Context that only one question
  needs, including an image, usually fits best in that question's instructions (the question text)
  or its criteria (the descriptions of its options, its levels, or what yes and no mean). Context
  that many questions share can go in the state once, and each question can refer to it by its
  exact path in backticks. When you ask the same question about many items, it usually works better
  to put each item into its own question than to give an ID the model has to look up in a shared
  list.
- **Each question is answered on its own.** Questions in a request can't see each other or each
  other's answers. Any context a question relies on belongs in the state or in that question.
- **Write plainly.** A question isn't an LLM prompt. Preambles, "consider X, Y, and Z" lists, and
  output-format instructions add noise. Descriptions of the options belong in the criteria, not in
  the question. Phrase the question so that a true answer means yes. Watch for double negatives,
  and for presuppositions such as "the next step".
- **Name the case that causes confusion.** If answers keep mixing up two outcomes, say in the
  criteria what separates them, using the specific case. For example, for "Is this a refund
  request?", note that a question about the refund policy is not a request. A vague exclusion such
  as "not other kinds of message" helps less, and can draw attention to the wrong answer.

### Criteria

- **Ask about the null case separately.** A Box always returns a location and a Choice always picks
  an option, even when nothing fits. Pair either one with a Noul in the same request that asks
  whether anything fits ("Is there a coffee mug in `photo`?", "Does `message` name any of our
  products?"), so code can tell when nothing does. As of Jev 1.14, this companion Noul usually works
  better than a "none of the above" option.
- **Option names are sent to the model; question IDs are not.** Names that describe the content
  (`refund_request`, `shipping_delay`) help the model. Positional names (`A`, `left`, `option_1`)
  give it nothing meaningful to go on and can bias the answer.
- **Keep options distinct and concrete.** Wording that options share with each other, or with the
  input, can pull probability toward those options. An option that covers several meanings is
  often worth splitting, because its probability can't tell code which meaning applied. Direction
  and magnitude usually work better as separate questions, so that the answer to one doesn't get
  mixed into the other.
- **Describe each Score level as a situation.** Each level should make sense when read on its own:
  "The customer mentions a minor inconvenience" rather than "More upset than the previous level".
- **Describe a Noul's `false` criterion as a concrete situation**, such as "the package arrived on
  time", rather than as "not late".
- **Use a Noul per statement when more than one can be true.** A Choice picks one option, so a
  message that is both a refund request and a complaint forces it to split probability between the
  two. Separate Nouls let each one be true on its own.

## Compose requests

**Bundle questions that share state.** A handy heuristic: if two calls would send the same state
with different questions, they can likely be one call. Questions are cheap and run in parallel, and
the state is read and paid for once. See
[parallel questions](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/parallel_questions.md).

**Ask speculatively**, meaning ask a question before you know whether you'll need its answer. A
question that only matters in some cases can go in the same request as the question that
identifies the case. Ask "Is `order` a return request?" and "Which item in `order.items` is being
returned?" together, and have code read the second answer only when the first is yes. The second
question doesn't need an "if" clause, because code handles the condition. See
[speculative fan-out](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/fan-out.md).

A second request is usually worth it when:

- code needs an answer to build the next state, fetch evidence, or choose the next options;
- a state field needed for one question measurably misleads another;
- different sets of questions need to be cached or versioned separately.

## Read the answers

### Confidence is rarely the gate

Naive implementations often use an answer's `confidence` as the check that decides whether code
acts. Confidence measures how concentrated an answer's probability distribution is, which is not
the same as how likely the answer is to be correct. Think about what the probabilities should look
like in your use case; another calculation over them may suit it better.

### Probabilities and thresholds

- **A probability is the likelihood that an answer is correct.** Jev isn't a calculator for
  probability problems. Ask it for judgments, and do any math on odds or probabilities in code. A
  Noul near 0.5 usually means the state doesn't settle the question.
- **The top answer is a good default**: the Choice's top option, or the Score's position.
- **0.7 and 0.3 make good starting thresholds for a Noul**: above 0.7 reads as yes, below 0.3 as no,
  and the band between means the question isn't settled, which can get its own row in the truth
  table. Adjust them when the application calls for it, and be wary of over-fitting them to a
  handful of test cases.
- **Look at Score distributions.** The Score's position can get pulled toward the middle and hide
  two-peaked answers, so look at the level probabilities before deciding which value your code
  reads.

## Test with the live API

Sending test requests to the live API is a great way to test questions against your data. Ask the
user for permission first. Get a budget for experimentation (TypeSafe is very inexpensive, so a
little can go a very long way), disclose what data will be sent (point out any personal or private
data), and say that their `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` will be used.

- Start with a few representative cases, plus hard ones and some whose answer is "no" or "nothing
  fits".
- Compare wordings by sending each variant as a separate question in one request, over the same
  state.
- Read individual answers, not only aggregates.
- Keep the exact request payload for each case so any result can be rerun.
- Check each change against cases you didn't use while tuning.

Make sure any agent that sends test requests has network access to the API endpoint.

### When an answer looks wrong

Check these, in this order:

1. the payload as actually sent;
2. the state, against the human test;
3. the options and candidates: is the right answer among them?
4. the scope of the questions: can each one be broken down into smaller judgments?
5. the wording.

If a clear question with complete state still gets an answer you're confident is wrong, check the
jaggedness page for the model you're using. It lists known weak spots and how to work around them.
If the behavior isn't listed, the TypeSafe team welcomes examples through the channel linked on
that page. In the meantime, work out an alternative approach with the user that avoids the weak
spot.

### Yellow flags

Typically, a good change is one that makes the definition clearer or improves the state. Check each
change on cases you didn't tune on. Wording written to produce a particular value is **prompt
gymnastics**, and it tends to break on new inputs and on the next model version. Some yellow flags:

- criteria that name specific test items, or that gain a clause for each failing case;
- caveats that explain away a model quirk;
- thresholds fitted to particular cases;
- tests that assert an exact probability;
- code that quietly overrides answers.

The structural fix is usually better state, a separate question, or code.

## Cookbooks

Each of these starting points combines questions to serve one goal. Ideas outside this list are
welcome.

- **Route and fill arguments.** One request identifies what the user is asking for and which
  values go in each argument. Code then calls the handler. See
  [function calling](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/function_calling.md) and
  [intent routing](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/intent-routing.md).
- **Select instead of generate.** Code finds candidate values or spans of text, the model picks
  the intended one, and code copies or normalizes it. See
  [value extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/pre_parsed_value_extraction_cookbook.md),
  [date extraction](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/date_extraction_cookbook.md), and
  [structure recovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoformat.md).
- **Find and judge evidence.** Retrieve candidates and ask how relevant each one is. See
  [line-by-line search](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/semantic_find.md),
  [re-ranking](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/rerank_typesafe.md), and
  [classifying RAG passages](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/classifying_rag_passages.md).
- **Turn answers into data.** Score each dimension once, then let code or users change the weights
  and views. If you have labeled outcomes, the answers can become features for a model. See
  [composite scoring](https://docs.typesafe.ai/patterns/composite-scoring.md) and
  [feature discovery](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/autoresearch_feature_discovery.md).
- **Verify and escalate.** Check claims or fields against their evidence, and send the cases that
  fail to a person or a reasoning model. See
  [citation checks](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/citation_check.md) and
  [extraction cascades](https://docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/sde_cascade.md).

The TypeSafe team is constantly adding cookbooks of well-tested patterns to the live documentation.
It's a good idea to check the [cookbooks index](https://docs.typesafe.ai/go/cookbooks.md) for one
that fits the problem you're solving.

result.output:
# Maester 3.0 report redesign

Status: built in `report/` (overview, action plan, all tests, product, framework, ATT&CK, pack, changes and
run views; tabbed test detail; small-run layout; product icons; Copy for AI). The result data it needs is
implemented. Not yet built: accepted risk, co-branding and WebMCP.

- To see it: `npm --prefix report run dev`, then open `?sample=suite` (a full run), `?sample=tenants` (five
  tenants), `?sample=one` or `?sample=2x` (a 2.x result). The first design was a single-file mock, which this
  build replaces and which is not in the repository.

The mock used the report's 3.0 sample (`report/src/lib/testResults.ts`, the Pora Inc. tenant) plus
data it synthesises so every 3.0 feature has something to show: 336 Zero Trust Assessment rows from
the pack's real `catalog.json`, 13 ASD rows, a seven-test community pack (`MP.CNT`), reason codes on
skipped rows, and a previous run for drift. These are marked as synthetic in the build script and are
not tenant data.

## Who reads the report and what they need

| Reader | Question | Where the mock answers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Admin who has to fix things | What do I fix first, and how? | Overview "Fix these first", Action plan, test sheet with the fix and a rerun command |
| Security lead or manager | How are we doing, and is it getting better? | Overview headline, failed by severity, changes since last run |
| Auditor or GRC | Which framework requirements do we meet? | Frameworks views: requirements met, not met, not run, no test |
| Security analyst | Which attack techniques are we exposed to? | ATT&CK view |
| Product owner | How is my product doing? | Product views, grouped by feature |
| Whoever ran it | Why didn't some tests run? | "Why N tests did not run" with the command that fixes each group, Run details |

The 2.x report answers the first and last questions with one table. 3.0 gives every test the
attributes to answer the rest, and the report should use them.

## What 3.0 added, and where the report shows it

| 3.0 feature | Result fields | Report |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Products and features | `Product`, `RelatedProduct`, `Feature` + `Taxonomy` | Products in the sidebar with icons; product page grouped by feature; "Also affects" |
| Areas | `Area` | Security areas strip on the overview; group-by in the test list |
| Severity, user impact, effort | `Severity`, `UserImpact`, `ImplementationCost` | Ranking, effort/impact matrix, quick wins |
| Frameworks | `Benchmark`, `Control` + framework files | One view per framework, requirement coverage |
| ATT&CK | `Mitre` + `Taxonomy.Attack` | Tactic/technique grid, each tile coloured by its tests |
| Reason codes | `ReasonCode`, `ReasonDetail` | Grouped "did not run" list with a fix command; callout on the test |
| Maester Packs | `Source = Custom`, `Package` | Packs section in the sidebar, one view per pack, pack-defined grouping |
| Pack reports | `Attachments` (`Add-MtReportAttachment`) | Reports section, sandboxed frame (as today) |
| Families | `ParentId`, `InstanceId` | Instances list under the family in the test sheet (not in the mock yet) |
| Lifecycle | `Lifecycle`, `ReplacedBy` | Shown in the sheet; deprecated tests get a "replaced by" link |
| Licences, services, permissions | `License`, `Service`, `Permission`, `TenantContext` | Sheet attributes; Run details |
| Multi-tenant merge | `Tenants[]` / `Partitions[]` | All tenants page (`/tenants`), tenant list in the sidebar, switcher in the top bar, Tenants tab on a test |
| Affected objects | `AffectedObjects` | Kept as a Reports view (not in the mock; sample has none) |
| Drift suite, `Compare-MtTestResult` | `MT.1060` rows; compare output | "Changes since last run" view (needs the previous run, see below) |

## Information architecture

The sidebar is built from a view registry. Every page, built in or from a pack, is a view with an
id, a group, a title, an optional count and a render function. Groups, in order:

1. **Summary**: Overview, Action plan, All tests
2. **Products**: one view per product that has results, with its icon and failed count
3. **Frameworks**: CIS Microsoft 365, CISA SCuBA, Essential Eight, NIST SP 800-53 (and any framework a
   pack or custom test maps to)
4. **Threats**: MITRE ATT&CK
5. **Packs**: one view per pack in the run, plus "Add a pack to the next run"
6. **Reports**: Changes since last run, embedded reports from packs, Affected objects, Run details

A test opens in a side sheet from anywhere, so the reader never loses their place. Search (⌘K)
finds views, tests, controls and techniques. Each view has a plain `#id` link for sharing.

### Overview

Headline sentence with the pass rate (passed ÷ (passed + failed); Investigate, skipped and not run are
not scored), counts by result, changes since the last run, failed by severity, the six tests to fix
first, product cards, framework coverage, security areas, why tests did not run, and the packs in the
run.

### Ranking: "Fix these first"

```
priority = 4 × severity (Critical 4 … Info 0)
         + 1.5 × (3 − user impact)      Low 2, Medium 1, High 0
         + 1.5 × (3 − effort)           Low 2, Medium 1, High 0
         + 0.3 × ATT&CK techniques (max 3)
         + 0.2 × framework requirements
```

Severity dominates; within a severity, cheap fixes users won't notice come first. A failure with
Medium or higher severity, Low user impact and Low effort is labelled a quick win. The Action plan
shows the 3×3 effort/impact matrix; choosing a cell lists its tests.

Open: a benchmark shim and the test it calls report the same setting twice. The plan should show one
row per setting, with the frameworks of both. That needs the shim relationship in the result (see
data changes).

### Frameworks

A framework view counts requirements, not tests: a requirement is met when every test for it passes,
not met when any fails, and "no Maester test" when nothing maps to it. Filters follow each framework's
own facts (CIS L1/L2, CISA SHALL/SHOULD, Essential Eight ML1–ML3). Groups follow the framework's
structure (CIS sections, CISA services, Essential Eight strategies, NIST control families).

### Packs

A pack's view shows its publisher, version, badges (Official, Microsoft MVP, GitHub-verified org) and
risk level, its results, its own grouping (ZTA: pillar and category), and any report it embedded. A
pack's results count in the report, never as Maester's own checks. Product cards say how many of their
tests came from packs.

### Small runs

The report adapts to the size of the run instead of showing empty charts. A view registers with a
condition and is left out of the sidebar when it has nothing to show. The mock's "Mock sample" menu
switches between a full run (673 tests), one suite (`-Suite CIS`, 25 tests) and one test.

| Run | What the reader sees |
| --- | --- |
| 1 to 3 tests | The tests themselves: the title as the headline, the verdict and how it compares with the last run in one sentence, each test's full detail inline, and commands to check more (`-Feature`, `-Product`, `-Suite`, everything). The sidebar has only Result and Run details. |
| A handful to one suite | The usual overview. Sections with nothing to show are left out: no Packs without packs, no Products card grid for one product, only the frameworks the tests map to. |
| Full run | Everything. |

The product, framework, ATT&CK and change views stay out of the sidebar for 1 to 3 tests: the test's own
tabs show its product, frameworks, techniques and history.

### The test view

A test opens in a side sheet (or inline for a small run) with a fixed header and tabs, so a long guide
never pushes the metadata out of reach:

- **Header**: result, ID, pack, "was passed last run", title, and key facts as chips with icons (product
  with its logo, severity, user impact, effort, area); rerun command, Docs, Copy for AI.
- **Finding**: what an attacker could do (from the test's area, in plain words), the reason it didn't run if
  it didn't, what Maester found, and why it matters (the guide up to its remediation heading).
- **How to fix**: the guide's remediation section, then the command to check it again.
- **Details**: every attribute, grouped (what it checks, impact, how it runs, where it comes from), each with
  its own icon; "Same check as" and "Also reported as" for shims.
- **Frameworks** and **ATT&CK** with counts in the tab; **History** compares with the previous run.

Each attribute has one icon used everywhere it appears (sheet, details, filters), drawn as one stroke set in the
report so no icon library is needed.

## Data changes the report needs

All additive to schema 2.1. Items 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 are implemented (see `website/docs/result-schema.md`);
item 4 is open.
