# Microsoft Entra deployment plans - Microsoft Entra | Microsoft Learn

Azure Active Directory is now [Microsoft Entra ID](../fundamentals/what-is-entra), which can safeguard your organization with cloud identity and access management. The solution connects employees, customers, and partners to their apps, devices, and data.

Use this article's guidance to help build your plan to deploy Microsoft Entra ID. Learn about plan-building basics and then use the following sections for authentication deployment, apps and devices, hybrid scenarios, user identity, and more.

Tip

**Looking for architecture diagrams and reference architectures?** For detailed architecture diagrams, hybrid identity topologies, and design guidance, see:

- [Microsoft Entra architecture overview](architecture) — service design, scalability, and availability
- [Build resilience in your hybrid architecture](resilience-in-hybrid) — architecture diagrams for PHS, PTA, and Federation
- [Choose the right authentication method](../identity/hybrid/connect/choose-ad-authn) — authentication decision tree
- [Identity and access management architecture in Azure](/en-us/azure/architecture/identity/identity-start-here) — reference architectures, baseline implementations, and design guidance
- [Data residency and sovereign cloud options](../fundamentals/data-residency) — data storage locations and environment constraints

## Stakeholders and roles

When beginning your deployment plans, include your key stakeholders. Identify and document stakeholders, affected roles, and the areas of ownership and responsibilities that enable an effective deployment. Titles and roles differ from one organization to another, however the ownership areas are similar. See the following table for common and influential roles that affect any deployment plan.

| Role | Responsibility |
| --- | --- |
| Sponsor | An enterprise senior leader with authority to approve or assign budget and resources. The sponsor is the connection between managers and the executive team. |
| End users | The people for whom the service is implemented. Users can participate in a pilot program. |
| IT Support Manager | Provides input on the supportability of proposed changes |
| Identity architect | Defines how the change aligns with identity management infrastructure |
| Application business owner | Owns the affected applications, which might include access management. Provides input on the user experience. |
| Security owner | Confirms the change plan meets security requirements |
| Compliance Manager | Ensures compliance with corporate, industry, or governmental requirements |

### RACI

Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed (responsible/accountable/consulted/informed (RACI)) is a model for the participation by various roles to complete tasks or deliverables for a project or business process. Use this model to help ensure the roles in your organization understand deployment responsibilities.

- **Responsible**- The people accountable for the correct completion of the task.
    - There is at least one Responsible role, although you can delegate others to help deliver the work.
- **Accountable** - The one ultimately answerable for the correctness and completion of the deliverable or task. The Accountable role ensures task prerequisites are met and delegates work to responsible roles. The Accountable role approves work that Responsible provides. Assign one Accountable for each task or deliverable.
- **Consulted** - The Consulted role provides guidance, typically a subject matter expert (SME).
- **Informed** - The people kept up to date on progress, generally upon completion of a task or deliverable.

## Authentication deployment

Use the following list to plan for authentication deployment.

- **Microsoft Entra multifactor authentication (MFA)** - Using admin-approved authentication methods, multifactor authentication helps safeguard access to your data and applications while meeting the demand for easy sign-in:

    - See the video, [How to configure and enforce multifactor authentication in your tenant](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qNndxl7gqVM)
    - See, [Plan a multifactor authentication deployment](../identity/authentication/howto-mfa-getstarted)
- **Conditional Access** - Implement automated access-control decisions for users to access cloud apps, based on conditions:

    - See, [What is Conditional Access?](../identity/conditional-access/overview)
    - See, [Plan a Conditional Access deployment](../identity/conditional-access/plan-conditional-access)
- **Microsoft Entra self-service password reset (SSPR)** - Help users reset a password without administrator intervention:

    - See, [Passkeys (FIDO2) authentication method in Microsoft Entra ID](../identity/authentication/concept-authentication-passkeys-fido2)
    - See, [Plan a Microsoft Entra self-service password-reset deployment](../identity/authentication/concept-sspr-deploy)
- **Passwordless authentication** - Implement passwordless authentication using the Microsoft Authenticator app or FIDO2 Security keys:

    - See, [Enable passwordless sign-in with Microsoft Authenticator](../identity/authentication/howto-authentication-passwordless-phone)
    - See, [Plan a passwordless authentication deployment in Microsoft Entra ID](../identity/authentication/howto-authentication-passwordless-deployment)

## Applications and devices

Use the following list to help deploy applications and devices.

- **Single sign-on (SSO)**- Enable user access to apps and resources with one sign-in, without reentering credentials:
    - See, [What is SSO in Microsoft Entra ID?](../identity/enterprise-apps/what-is-single-sign-on)
    - See, [Plan a SSO deployment](../identity/enterprise-apps/plan-sso-deployment)
- **My Apps portal**- Discover and access applications. Enable user productivity with self-service, for instance request access to groups, or manage access to resources on behalf of others.
    - See, [My Apps portal overview](../identity/enterprise-apps/myapps-overview)
- **Devices**- Evaluate device integration methods with Microsoft Entra ID, choose the implementation plan, and more.
    - See, [Plan your Microsoft Entra device deployment](../identity/devices/plan-device-deployment)

## Hybrid scenarios

For architecture diagrams and resilience patterns for hybrid identity deployments, see [Build resilience in your hybrid architecture](resilience-in-hybrid). For full reference architectures with downloadable Visio diagrams, see [Integrate on-premises Active Directory with Microsoft Entra ID](/en-us/azure/architecture/reference-architectures/identity/azure-ad).

The following list describes features and services in hybrid scenarios.

- **Active Directory Federation Services (AD FS)**- Migrate user authentication from federation to cloud with pass-through authentication or password hash sync:
    - See, [What is federation with Microsoft Entra ID?](../identity/hybrid/connect/whatis-fed)
    - See, [Migrate from federation to cloud authentication](../identity/hybrid/connect/migrate-from-federation-to-cloud-authentication)
- **Microsoft Entra application proxy**- Enable employees to be productive from a device. Learn about software as a service (SaaS) apps in the cloud and corporate apps on-premises. Microsoft Entra application proxy enables access without virtual private networks (VPNs) or demilitarized zones (DMZs):
    - See, [Remote access to on-premises applications through Microsoft Entra application proxy](../identity/app-proxy/overview-what-is-app-proxy)
    - See, [Plan a Microsoft Entra application proxy deployment](../identity/app-proxy/conceptual-deployment-plan)
- **Seamless single sign-on (Seamless SSO)**- Use Seamless SSO for user sign-in, on corporate devices connected to a corporate network. Users don't need passwords to sign in to Microsoft Entra ID, and usually don't need to enter usernames. Authorized users access cloud-based apps without extra on-premises components:
    - See, [Microsoft Entra SSO: Quickstart](../identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-sso-quick-start)
    - See, [Microsoft Entra seamless SSO: Technical deep dive](../identity/hybrid/connect/how-to-connect-sso-how-it-works)

## Users

- **User identities**- Learn about automation to create, maintain, and remove user identities in cloud apps, such as Dropbox, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and more.
    - See, [Plan an automatic user provisioning deployment in Microsoft Entra ID](../identity/app-provisioning/plan-auto-user-provisioning)
- **Microsoft Entra ID Governance**- Create identity governance and enhance business processes that rely on identity data. With HR products, such as Workday or Successfactors, manage employee and contingent-staff identity lifecycle with rules. These rules map Joiner-Mover-Leaver (JLM) processes, such as New Hire, Terminate, Transfer, to IT actions such as Create, Enable, Disable. See the following section for more.
    - See, [Plan cloud HR application to Microsoft Entra user provisioning](../identity/app-provisioning/plan-cloud-hr-provision)
- **Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration**- Improve external-user collaboration with secure access to applications:
    - See, [B2B collaboration overview](../external-id/what-is-b2b)
    - See, [Plan a Microsoft Entra B2B collaboration deployment](secure-external-access-resources)

## Identity Governance and reporting

[Microsoft Entra ID Governance](../id-governance/identity-governance-overview) enables organizations to improve productivity, strengthen security and more easily meet compliance and regulatory requirements. Use Microsoft Entra ID Governance to ensure the right people have the right access to the right resources. Improve identity and access process automation, delegation to business groups, and increased visibility. Use the following list to learn about identity governance and reporting.

Learn more:

- [Secure access for a connected world—meet Microsoft Entra](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/?p=114039)
- [Govern access for applications in your environment](../id-governance/identity-governance-applications-prepare)
- **Privileged Identity Management (PIM)** - Manage privileged administrative roles across Microsoft Entra ID, Azure resources, and other Microsoft online services. Use it for just-in-time (JIT) access (JIT), request approval workflows, and integrated access reviews to help prevent malicious activities:

    - See, [Start using Privileged Identity Management](../id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-getting-started)
    - See, [Plan a Privileged Identity Management deployment](../id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-deployment-plan)
- **Reporting and monitoring** - The Microsoft Entra reporting and monitoring solution design has dependencies and constraints: legal, security, operations, environment, and processes.

    - See, [Microsoft Entra reporting and monitoring deployment dependencies](../identity/monitoring-health/plan-monitoring-and-reporting)
- **Access reviews** - Understand and manage access to resources:

    - See, [What are access reviews?](../id-governance/access-reviews-overview)
    - See, [Plan a Microsoft Entra access reviews deployment](../id-governance/deploy-access-reviews)

## Best practices for a pilot

Before making a change for larger groups, or everyone, use pilots to test with a small group. Ensure each use case in your organization is tested.

### Pilot: Phase 1

In your first phase, target IT, usability, and other users who can test and provide feedback. Use this feedback to gain insights on potential issues for support staff, and to develop communications and instructions you send to all users.

### Pilot: Phase 2

Widen the pilot to larger groups of users by using dynamic membership, or by manually adding users to the targeted groups.

Learn more: [Dynamic membership rules for groups in Microsoft Entra ID](../identity/users/groups-dynamic-membership)

# Zero Trust deployment for technology pillars overview | Microsoft Learn

This article summarizes technology pillars in our [Zero Trust adoption model](../security-adoption-model).

Technology pillars represent the core areas of your security architecture. They group related capabilities and controls into logical domains such as identity, endpoints, data, apps, infrastructure, networks, and security operations.

Each pillar answers the same fundamental question:

**How do we apply Zero Trust principles to this part of the environment?**

Instead of thinking in terms of individual products or features, pillars provide a stable way to organize security design and implementation across your environment.

![Diagram of elements of visibility, automation, and orchestration in Zero Trust.](../media/diagram-zero-trust-security-elements.png)

## Technology pillars in the adoption model

Our structured adoption model focuses on three components:

- [Business scenarios](../security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview) - Define the most critical security outcomes for the organization. They focus on **why** we're adopting Zero Trust security.
- [Security disciplines](../security-adoption-discipline-overview) - Guide teams to define strategy, architecture, processes, and controls across common areas of security so that we can deliver the business scenarios. They focus on **what** Zero Trust capabilities are required.
- **Technology pillars** - Secure specific areas of the organization such as identity, data, and devices. They focus on **where** security capabilities are implemented.
- [Technical solutions](../implement-overview) - As adoption moves towards deployment, technical solutions provide detailed guidance for implementing security controls across technology pillars. They focus on **how** security is implemented.

In the Zero Trust adoption model, technology pillars sit between strategy and implementation.

Technology pillars don't define outcomes (business solutions) or steps (technical solutions), but they do:

- Define technical boundaries where security controls are applied. These boundaries are used by solutions to organize implementation guidance and logic.
- Act as the bridge between intent (why) and implementation (how).

## Pillars

| Technology pillar | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [![Fingerprint icon](../media/icon-identity-small.png)](identity)[Identities](identity) | Control access decisions. Every request starts with identity verification and enforcement of least privilege. |
| [![Endpoints icon.](../media/icon-endpoints-small.png)](endpoints)[Endpoints](endpoints) | Evaluate and enforce device trust. Access depends on device health, compliance, and risk. |
| [![Ones and zeroes icon.](../media/icon-data-small.png)](data)[Data](data) | Protect the asset itself. Security persists with the data through classification, labeling, encryption, and access control. |
| [![Application window icon.](../media/icon-applications-small.png)](applications)[Apps](applications) | Govern how data is accessed. Apply controls at the application and API layer, including permissions and session controls. |
| [![Data storage disks icon.](../media/icon-infrastructure-small.png)](infrastructure)[Infrastructure](infrastructure) | Secure compute resources. Harden servers, VMs, containers, and services through configuration, access control, and monitoring. |
| [![Network diagram icon.](../media/icon-networks-small.png)](networks)[Network](networks) | Control connectivity and movement. Segment and monitor traffic to prevent lateral movement and enforce secure communication. |
| [![Gear icon.](../media/icon-visibility-automation-orchestration-small.png)](visibility-automation-orchestration)[SecOps](visibility-automation-orchestration) | Integrate and operationalize all pillars. Detect, investigate, and respond using signals from across the environment. |

## Zero Trust implementation workshops

Microsoft's Zero Trust implementation workshops are available for each pillar. [Learn more](../workshop-zero-trust-overview).

## What's next?

- [Review](../implement-overview) technical solutions.
- [Learn about](../security-adoption-model) our Zero Trust adoption model.
- [Review](../security-adoption-business-scenarios-overview) critical security business scenarios.

function Resolve-MtNativePlan {
    <#
    .SYNOPSIS
    Decides, for every native test, whether it runs and if not why (design stages 5 and 6).
    .DESCRIPTION
    Gates apply in this order, and the first failing gate gives the reason (design section 6):
    invalid metadata; disabled by config; selection (IDs, excluded products, typed selectors, tags, opt-in
    service, Preview, long-running); platform; tenant type; cloud; service; licence; parameter binding.
    The default exclusions are decided by attribute, not by tag (test attribute design, section 4): a test
    with Lifecycle = 'Preview' or LongRunning is left out when the run excludes them by default
    (-AutoExcludedTag) and the test is not named by its exact ID, and a test whose service is opt-in, such
    as Active Directory, when that service is not connected.
    Each plan row has: Test, Disposition (Run, NotRun, Skipped or Error), ReasonCode, ReasonDetail,
    LegacySkipCode, Parameters (the bound hashtable), EffectiveParameters, TimeoutSeconds, Setting (the
    TestSettings row), InstancePatterns (for a family selected by instance ID) and ExactlyNamed.
    #>
    [CmdletBinding()]
    [OutputType([pscustomobject])]
    param(
        [Parameter(Mandatory)] [AllowEmptyCollection()] [object[]] $Test,
        [Parameter(Mandatory)] [pscustomobject] $Selection,
        [Parameter(Mandatory)] [pscustomobject] $RunConfig,
        [Parameter()] [AllowNull()] [pscustomobject] $TenantContext,
        # The include and exclude tags of the run, and which exclusions the engine added by default

        [Parameter()] [string[]] $IncludeTag = @(),
        [Parameter()] [string[]] $ExcludeTag = @(),
        [Parameter()] [string[]] $AutoExcludedTag = @(),
        # Parameter values that win over the config (Invoke-MtTest -Parameter), by test ID.
        [Parameter()] [hashtable] $ParameterOverride = @{},
        [Parameter()] [switch] $DryRun
    )
    $environment = if ($RunConfig.PSObject.Properties['Environment']) { $RunConfig.Environment } else { $null }
    $enforce = @{ Service = $true; License = $true; TenantType = $false; Cloud = $false }
    if ($environment -and $environment.PSObject.Properties['Enforce'] -and $environment.Enforce) {

Where the seven chains came from

I chose them by hand. They're the deployments where Microsoft's guidance is most explicit about order, and where the wrong order locks users out. I matched each against the titles of Maester's 893 checks and the Zero Trust pack's catalogue. Three were confirmed against Microsoft Learn in this research: compliant devices, risk policies and token protection. The other four (PIM, phishing-resistant MFA, email authentication and Defender risk) come from Microsoft guidance I know and still need the same check. Treat the table as a worked example, not a finished catalogue.

More chains to look at

ChainOrder of changesChecks that map to it
Block legacy authenticationFind legacy sign-ins → move clients to modern auth → block in CAMT.1009, MT.1010, MT.1033, plus measured impact (B1)
Guest and external accessCross-tenant access defaults → limits on who can invite → MFA for guests → access reviews for guestsMT.1016, ZTA.21857, EIDSCA authorization settings
App consentAdmin consent workflow → restrict user consent → review existing grantsEIDSCA.AP09, EIDSCA.CP03, CIS consent checks
Workload credentialsCertificates, managed identities or federated credentials → remove secrets → limit credential lifetimes → app owners have MFA, or privileged apps have no ownersMT.1057, MT.1198, MT.1199, MT.1063, MT.1077, MT.1078
Hybrid identity hardeningPassword hash sync → block soft and hard matching → turn off seamless SSO → cloud-only adminsCIS.M365.5.1.8.1, MT.1073, MT.1084, MT.1026, MT.1081, MT.1147
Self-service password resetSSPR → password writeback → feeds remediation in the risk chainNone found by title: a gap
Local admin and LAPSEntra join → LAPS → limit local admins at join → restrict BitLocker key recoveryCIS.M365.5.1.4.3–5.1.4.6, MT.1090, MT.1091, ZTA.21955
Data protectionSensitivity labels for groups and sites → publish labels → default and automatic labels → DLP in simulation → enforceThe 10 Purview checks
SharePoint sharingTenant sharing level → anyone links off or expiring → default link type → site overridesThe 20 SharePoint checks
Audit and detectionUnified audit log → mailbox auditing → alert policies → diagnostic settings to a SIEMMT.1172, MT.1100. Maester's own log reads (B1, B2) depend on this chain too.
Defender for Office 365Preset policies → priority accounts → impersonation protectionZTA.41033 and ORCA checks. Needs a VIP list, which C1 could suggest.
Global Secure AccessClient deployed → traffic forwarding profiles → compliant network in CA → private access apps behind CA with a managed deviceZTA.25372, MT.1187, MT.1189, ZTA.25379, MT.1188, MT.1193
AI agentsAgent inventory with sponsors → limit Graph permissions → block high agent riskMT.1223, MT.1181, Copilot Studio checks MT.1113–MT.1122
Later: GitHub, Azure DevOps, Active DirectoryEach gets its own entries. AD tiering is a large set of chains on its own.270 AD checks, CIS GitHub

Finding chains systematically

  • Microsoft's deployment plans. Entra publishes about 16 "Plan a … deployment" pages (MFA, Conditional Access, SSPR, passwordless, devices, PIM, access reviews, B2B and others), and Intune, Purview and Defender have their own. Each has prerequisites. They're the backbone of the catalogue.
  • The Learn pages Maester already links. That's 514 pages from 474 check guides. Mine them for "before", "first" and "must".
  • The Zero Trust pack's remediation text for its 336 checks.
  • Microsoft's pilot pattern (a small pilot, then wider groups, then everyone). It gives the rollout steps for every Conditional Access change.
  • Later, co-failure data: which checks tend to fail together across many tenants. This needs data from many tenants, so it's out of scope for the open-source report.

Estimate: 20 to 25 chains of 60 to 80 changes, mapping 250 to 350 checks. The rest of the checks stand alone.

Work in another session

Object facts, and what they change here

The session "Zero trust data in affected objects" (branch feat/zta-affected-object-facts, not committed yet) adds a public command, Add-MtAffectedObjectFact. Each fact has a name, a value shown as text, a tone (Risk, Warning, Good or Info), a source and the date its data was read. Facts attach to objects the run already lists. The Zero Trust pack reads its tenant export and adds facts to apps (permissions, consent, last sign-in, owners, credentials), users (roles, MFA, passwordless, last sign-in), devices (OS, join type, managed and compliant), agents (sponsors, owners) and Intune policies (assignments, last changed).

Part of this planWhat the facts change
A2, most exposed identitiesFacts supply the weights: privileged roles, MFA not registered, dormant accounts, risky permissions. The Affected objects page with facts is the start of the object pages. A2 still needs to know why each check named an object.
Readiness in the defender's pathDevice facts (join type, managed and compliant) and user facts (MFA, passwordless) are readiness for each object, which is the drill-down behind a lane: "these 38 devices aren't managed". They can't give tenant-wide shares, because facts attach only to listed objects and come from the Zero Trust export only when it ran. Readiness checks still read Graph themselves, and should write facts too.
Tier C, question modelsModel answers become facts, with the model as the source and the tone Warning, such as "Looks like a service account". A reader's correction attaches to the same fact.
Unknown and datesFacts carry the date their data was read, so a readiness figure from an earlier Zero Trust export shows that date.
PrivacyEvery reader sees the facts, and redaction covers only user names the run knows. The same limit applies to classifying job titles (C1).

One request before the command ships, since it becomes public API: give each fact a stable key and a raw value next to its display text. Examples: user.mfaRegistered = false, signIn.daysSince = 143, device.joinType = hybrid, roles.privileged = true. Add a short shared list of keys too. Insights and readiness can then compute from facts without parsing English. It can be added later without breaking anything, but it costs less now.

Alignment

Small runs, and runs outside the chains

Many runs aren't full runs. A user runs one check, one suite, or only GitHub or Azure DevOps checks that no chain covers. The rule for the report, the console and the output files is the same: scope everything to what ran, and never infer a status for a check that didn't run.

RunReportConsoleOutput files
Full runA lane for every chain that has a check in the run. The overview opens with what's ready and what's blocked.One summary line: "2 changes ready, 1 blocked by ZTA.24542"Steps in the JSON. Step and blocked-by columns in the CSV and Markdown.
One suite or productOnly chains with a check in the run. A change whose checks weren't selected shows "Not checked in this run", with the command to include them.The line appears only when a chain is in scopeSteps lists the changes in scope, with all their checks
1 to 3 checksNo lanes. Each check shows "Before you fix this": its prerequisites, each with its status from this run, from an earlier run in the output folder (with its date), or Not checked.Nothing extraThe same
Checks in no chain (GitHub, Azure DevOps, AD, most custom checks)Nothing changes. The view stays hidden, as views without data already are.NothingNo Steps
Checks that couldn't run (service not connected, no licence)Unknown, with the reason and the fix command. Never Not done.Counted with the checks that didn't runStatus Unknown, with the reason code
Report · One check · MT.1001Example data

Before you fix this

2 of 4 prerequisites not confirmed
Devices enroll in Intune automatically (passed in the full run on 2 Nov)ZTA.24546
A compliance policy covers every platform (failed on 2 Nov)ZTA.24542
Emergency access accounts are excluded (this run)MT.1005
Windows devices are joined (not checked)No check yet
Invoke-Maester -Step ca-require-compliant-device -IncludePrerequisites
  • Three statuses that must not blur: Not done (the check failed), Unknown (the check couldn't run), and Not checked (the run didn't select it). Headline numbers never count a change that wasn't checked.
  • Always give the command that fills the gap. The report already does this for checks that didn't run, and the defender's path adds -Step and -IncludePrerequisites to the selectors.
  • Build Steps from the full inventory, not just the rows that ran. That's the same way Frameworks comes from the framework files. The report then knows every check that maps to a change in scope, even ones the run didn't select.
  • Status from earlier runs needs results for each check from more than the newest earlier run. That's the same change as A4. An earlier status always shows its date, and is never mixed into this run's numbers.
  • Custom checks and packs can name a step to join a chain. GitHub, Azure DevOps and AD chains come later as entries of their own, and until then those runs look as they do today.

input.ask: Should I send the fact-key suggestion to the Zero Trust facts session?

content.text:
I've updated [the plan page](https://claude.ai/artifact/Xtiz4DyW2n7MEwZujQbNAG) (version 4) with all three.

## How the object-facts work changes this plan

The other session ([Zero trust data in affected objects](#local_1ccd8527-10ab-4eb5-9783-856fbd0f2c6c)) has uncommitted work on `feat/zta-affected-object-facts`. It adds a public command, `Add-MtAffectedObjectFact`, which attaches facts to objects the run already lists. Each fact has a name, a value shown as text, a tone (Risk, Warning, Good or Info), a source and the date its data was read. The Zero Trust pack uses it to fill in roles, MFA, last sign-in, app permissions, device join type and whether a device is managed and compliant.

It fits this plan closely:
- **Most exposed identities:** facts supply the weights (privileged roles, no MFA, dormant accounts, risky permissions). The Affected objects page with facts becomes the start of the per-object pages.
- **Readiness:** device and user facts are per-object readiness, which is exactly what a chain's details need ("these 38 devices aren't managed"). They can't give tenant-wide percentages: facts only attach to objects the run lists, and the Zero Trust export exists only when that pack ran. So readiness checks still read Graph themselves, and should write facts too.
- **Model answers:** they become facts with the model as the source, and a reader's correction attaches to the same fact.

**One gap, worth fixing before it ships, since it becomes public API:** a fact's value is display text only. Give each fact a stable key and a raw value, such as `user.mfaRegistered` = false or `device.joinType` = hybrid. Otherwise the insights have to parse English to compute anything.

## Where the seven chains came from

I chose them by hand. They're the deployments where Microsoft's guidance is clearest about order, and where the wrong order locks users out. I then matched them against the titles of the 893 checks and the Zero Trust pack's catalogue.

Only three are confirmed against Microsoft Learn so far: compliant devices, risk policies and token protection. PIM, phishing-resistant MFA, email authentication and Defender risk come from guidance I know, and still need that check. Treat the seven as a worked example, not a finished list.

**More chains to look at** (14 on the page, with check IDs):
- Blocking legacy authentication, guest access and app consent.
- Workload credentials: from secrets to certificates or managed identities, then credential lifetimes and app owners.
- Hybrid identity hardening: password hash sync, soft and hard matching, seamless SSO.
- Self-service password reset: no check exists yet.
- LAPS and local admin, Purview labels to DLP, SharePoint sharing, and audit and detection. Maester's own log reads depend on that last one.
- Defender for Office 365, Global Secure Access, and AI agents.
- Later, GitHub, Azure DevOps and Active Directory.

**To find chains systematically:**
- Entra's own deployment plans: about 16 "Plan a … deployment" pages, each with prerequisites. Intune, Purview and Defender have the same kind of guides.
- The 514 Learn pages Maester's guides already link to.
- The Zero Trust pack's remediation text.

My rough guess is 20 to 25 chains covering 250 to 350 checks. The rest of the checks stand alone.

## One check, or GitHub-only runs

The rule for the report, the console and the output files is the same: scope everything to what ran, and never infer a status for a check that didn't run.
- **Three statuses kept apart:**
  - **Not done:** the check failed.
  - **Unknown:** the check couldn't run, for example a service wasn't connected.
  - **Not checked:** the run didn't select it.

  Headline numbers never count a change that wasn't checked.
- **One to three checks:** no chain view. Each check gets a "Before you fix this" box listing its prerequisites. Each shows its status from this run, or from an earlier run with that run's date, or "Not checked". The box ends with a command to check the rest, such as `Invoke-Maester -Step ca-require-compliant-device -IncludePrerequisites`.
- **GitHub, Azure DevOps, AD or custom checks that belong to no chain:** nothing changes. The view stays hidden, the console prints nothing extra, and the JSON has no `Steps`.
- **One suite or product:** only chains with a check in the run appear. A change whose checks weren't selected says so, with the command to include them.
- **One implementation rule:** build `Steps` from the full list of checks, the way `Frameworks` is built from the framework files. Then the report knows every check behind a change, even ones the run didn't select.

The page now has 13 decisions, including fact keys and the "Not checked" status.
